                                          "Sarah M., Top Producer in Austin, TX"

                                          "Jennifer K., Miami Real Estate Agent"
  plus "Mike R." on /instagram-bio-for-realtors and "David K." on
  /features/analytics.
The clincher: "Sarah M." is simultaneously a Luxury Agent in Austin TX, a Top
Producer in Austin TX, and from Beverly Hills. Same initials, three different
biographies. These were not left in place out of doubt about what they are —
they sit outside US-156's scope and removing marketing copy across six more

### US-157 — structured data — 2026-09-08 — PASSES

The story described 3 Product-snippet impressions and asked for deliberate
coverage. What the audit actually found was that the site was publishing false
claims to search, and had been since before US-111.

INVENTED STAR RATINGS ON 31 PAGES. Every one carried
`aggregateRating: {ratingValue: "4.8", reviewCount: "523"}`. US-111 had already
identified this exact pair as "both invented", removed it from the landing page,
and left a comment saying why — but missed five other sources that were still
emitting it: seo.ts (three separate literals), PageSEO.tsx, and
SEO_CONFIG.ratings, which fed all 23 city pages through LocationTemplate. Google
renders stars in search results from this field, so the site was showing a
fabricated 4.8-from-523-reviews to everyone who searched. AggregateRating count
in the built output: 31 before, 0 after.

The genuinely data-driven ones were kept. FullProfilePage and ReviewSchema
compute ratings from the `testimonials` table — real reviews of a real agent —
and are untouched. generateSoftwareApplicationSchema was emitting an
aggregateRating with `undefined` values because SchemaMarkup calls it without
ratings; it is now conditional, so absent rather than malformed.

A FALSE PRICE FOR A NAMED PLAN. The literal '39' appeared in five places, and
seo.config.ts:230 attached it to a node explicitly named "Professional" —
which costs 49. The homepage's SoftwareApplication Offer also published price
'39'. There is no $39 plan; the matrix is 0, 29, 49, 99, 299. This is the same
phantom figure US-156 found on /vs/linktree, which suggests it was once a real
price and nothing propagated the change. Every occurrence now derives from
PRICING_PLANS. The homepage's single Offer became an AggregateOffer with
lowPrice 29 / highPrice 299, which is the honest shape for a tiered product.
Verified in the built output: the only offer values now are 0, 29 and 29-299.

EIGHTEEN FAQ QUESTIONS MARKED UP BUT NOT ON THE PAGE, across six pages —
/vs/linktree, /vs/beacons, /for-real-estate-agents, /instagram-bio-for-realtors
and both free tools. FAQPage schema describing content a visitor cannot see is a
structured-data policy violation and a manual-action risk. Rather than delete
the markup, the answers were already written, so they are now rendered:
src/components/seo/FaqSection.tsx takes one array per page and produces both the
JSON-LD (faqPageSchema) and the visible <details> list. They cannot drift,
because they are the same array. Confirmed in the built HTML that the questions
appear in the rendered text with the <script> content stripped out.

BreadcrumbList was missing from /vs/linktree, /vs/beacons and /vs/later while
/features/*, /for/* and the tools all had one. Added; 52 -> 55 in the output.
/features/analytics has no '@graph' schema block at all, so it was left alone
rather than restructured — noted here rather than half-done.

The check that keeps all of this true: scripts/lib/seo-audit.mjs now parses
every JSON-LD block in the built HTML and fails on unparseable JSON, on the
4.8/523 pair specifically, on an aggregateRating missing ratingValue or
reviewCount, and on a FAQPage question absent from the rendered text. Proven
against the real build rather than asserted — a malformed block, a reinstated
4.8/523, and an invented FAQ question ("Does AgentBio secretly cure baldness
overnight?") each failed it with the right message, and the restored build
passes.

That last check had a bug worth recording. The first version stripped HTML tags
but not <script> CONTENT, so a FAQ question trivially "appeared on the page" by
matching its own JSON-LD source, and the baldness question passed. Fixing it
immediately surfaced all 18 real cases. A check that cannot fail is worse than
no check, and this one could not fail until it was tested against something that
should fail.

No Review or aggregateRating schema was added anywhere. Seven hardcoded,
unverifiable testimonials are still live elsewhere on the site (listed under the
US-156 entry); emitting review markup from them would have converted a content
problem into a structured-data misrepresentation.

Verification: build exits 0 (51 routes), verify:seo passes all 51 with the new
structured-data rules, tsc --noEmit clean, impeccable clean on FaqSection.

Test suite: 632 passed / 13 failed at 90s — the load-flaky pattern again, and I
checked it properly this time because a lot of pages changed. Run as a group of
seven, eight failed; run ONE AT A TIME, every single one passed: SubmitReview
5/5, Settings 6/6, LeadDetailModal 7/7, Register 3/3, ContactForm 3/3.
routes.test.ts passed in both the group and alone. The stable floor remains
repo-hygiene x2, analytics and analyticsEvents.

### US-158 — link acquisition programme — 2026-09-08 — PASSES

The artefacts are built. NOBODY HAS BEEN CONTACTED, no account was created, no
listing was submitted, and no placement exists. That half is a person's and is
written up as such.

THE RESEARCH CHANGED THE PLAN. Searching "best link in bio tools for real estate
agents 2026" on 2026-09-08 returned a first page dominated by COMPETITOR-OWNED
content marketing, not neutral roundups — linqin.in, simplelistings.co,
direct.me (twice), clientkeepercrm.com and linkship.cc are all competing
products marketing themselves. A competitor will not add us to their roundup,
and pitching them only tells them we exist. That SERP is won by publishing a
better page than theirs, which is what US-155 and US-156 started, not by
outreach.

The real targets are one step out, and every URL in Tier 1 was actually
retrieved rather than guessed: HousingWire's marketing-tools, software and
AI-tools roundups; The Close's software and apps roundups; Inman's AI-tools
piece. Tier 2 (G2, Capterra/GetApp/Software Advice, Product Hunt) and Tier 3
(r/realtors, agent Facebook groups, brokerages, state associations) are listed
as CATEGORIES and the doc says plainly that their submission routes were NOT
opened or verified — treating an unverified link as checked is how a target list
becomes fiction. No contact names or email addresses are listed, because I
verified none and a wrong name is worse than no name.

/press ships, prerendered, in the sitemap, linked from the footer so it is not
orphaned the way the comparison pages were. Every claim is checkable: what the
product does (five capabilities, each linking to its feature page), who it is
for, and what it costs — with the price table read from PRICING_PLANS so it
cannot drift from the checkout. Verified in the built HTML that it carries $0,
$29, $49, $99 and $299 and NONE of 4.8, 523, "2,000+", $39 or $19. No customer
counts, no funding, no awards, no press mentions, no ratings, no testimonials.
The page says so where a reader would expect one.

Product screenshots are deliberately absent. Real ones need a populated account
and a person to choose what to show; generating something representative would
mean inventing an agent's listings, which is the same failure as the fabricated
testimonials. The page asks the reader to request current ones instead.

Three sendable templates in docs/seo/OUTREACH_TEMPLATES.md — roundup author,
directory submission, partnership. They carry no invented social proof, they
name the specific article, they say out loud where a competitor is the better
choice, and there is no follow-up sequence. The directory template tells the
sender to check the price against /pricing rather than typing it from memory,
because typing it from memory is exactly how $39 ended up in six places
describing a plan that does not exist.

docs/seo/SEO_RECOVERY_CHECKLIST.md is the single owner-facing page: what eleven
stories changed, and the seven things only a person can do, ordered by damage.
Removing the seven remaining fabricated testimonials is first, and the link
document says explicitly not to pitch HousingWire until it is done — a reviewer
who checks one quoted agent and finds nothing will not check the second.

A REAL REGRESSION, CAUGHT BY CHECKING IN ISOLATION. routes.test.ts began failing
after the press page was added, and unlike every other suspect this batch it
failed ALONE, not only under load. The page links six logo files (/logo.png,
/Cover.webp and so on) and the test's link scanner measured them against the
route table, reporting each as a link to a non-existent route. They are static
assets in public/ that React Router never sees. Fixed in the test rather than in
the page — it now skips paths with a file extension, the same rule
isReservedSegment already uses in functions/_lib/social-meta.ts. Confirmed the
check still has teeth by pointing a link at /this-route-does-not-exist: it
failed, and passed again once restored.

Verification: build exits 0 (52 routes), verify:seo passes all 52, tsc --noEmit
clean, impeccable clean on Press.tsx. The full suite gave 20 failures at 103s —
the worst run of the batch and also its slowest — but run in isolation the four
files give exactly the four stable pre-existing failures (repo-hygiene x2,
analytics, analyticsEvents) and routes.test.ts passes 3/3.

### US-159 — remove every fabricated claim — 2026-09-08 — PASSES

Authorised by Dj: "No fabricated text, we need to remove false claims and false
testimonies." This is the third pass at the same defect, and the first one that
swept the whole of src/ rather than the pages a story happened to touch.

WHAT THE SWEEP FOUND, beyond the seven testimonials already flagged:

  Five different invented agent counts, plus the original still live:
    2,847        instagram-bio-analyzer capture modal (twice)
    4,200+       listing-description-generator modal and page (four places)
    2,000+       /vs/beacons and /vs/linktree
    3,000+       /vs/later
    10,000+      /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer
    5,000+       /for-real-estate-agents and /instagram-bio-for-realtors
  US-111 documented "2,500+ vs 5,000+ on two pages one click apart" as the
  original defect. 5,000+ was still on two landing pages, untouched, and four
  more numbers had been added since.

  Hardcoded ratings: "4.9/5 rating" in both capture modals, and a
  "4.9/5 Agent Rating" stat tile on the analyzer page.

  "Used by agents at Keller Williams, Coldwell Banker, RE/MAX" — three real
  firms named as customers. A claim about them as much as about us.

  Four stat tiles on /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer: "2,847+ Agents Analyzed",
  "3X Average Lead Increase", "$50M+ In Deals Generated", "4.9/5 Agent Rating".
  Replaced with four things the tool actually does — 5 scored categories, 3
  rewrites, free, ~60s.

  Eight more named testimonials: three on the listing-description-generator
  page, one in each capture modal, and two whole fabricated sections —
  "Success Stories from {city} Agents" in LocationTemplate, which rendered two
  fictional agents with "3 closings", "15 leads/month", "$2M+ in sales" and
  "10x engagement" on ALL 26 city pages, each claiming to be local; and a
  four-testimonial "Agent Success Stories" block on /vs/later.

  And the worst of it, because it goes to real inboxes: the Instagram bio
  analyzer email drip quoted invented percentile benchmarks ("Average Agent:
  ~7 leads/month", "Top Performer: ~45 leads/month"), a section headed "Real
  results from ${market} agents" listing "Agent A: 3 -> 18 leads/month (6X)"
  and "Agent B: 8 -> 31 (4X)", "10,000+ real estate professionals trust us",
  "Average user generates 15+ leads/month" and "847 agents closed deals from
  AgentBio leads last month alone". All removed; the surrounding copy was
  rewritten to make the same point without inventing numbers.

WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY KEPT, with the reason recorded in the new test's
ALLOWED_FILES so the next sweep does not re-litigate it:
  - BioAnalyzerForm's "0 / 1-3 / 4-10 / 10+ leads/month" dropdown — it asks the
    visitor about their own current situation. Not a claim.
  - "Keller Williams, Coldwell Banker, etc." as the placeholder in a "your
    brokerage" input. An example of what to type.
  - features/Testimonials' "Star display (4.8/5.0, 4.9/5.0, etc.)" — product
    documentation for the testimonial widget, listed beside "Automatically
    updates as you add reviews".
  - The ExampleBio demos and bio-generator's suggested credentials
    ("$50M+ in luxury sales") — illustrations of what an agent might write about
    themselves, not claims about us.
  - Zapier's own published "5,000+ apps" figure in the integration modal.
  - ReviewSchema and FullProfilePage's aggregateRating, computed from the real
    `testimonials` table.
Nothing was reworded into a vaguer version of the same claim. A claim either had
something behind it or it went.

THE GUARD. src/marketing-claims.test.ts fails the build on any of five shapes:
a hardcoded named testimonial, a customer count, a star rating, an outcome
metric, or another company named as a customer. Three cleanups in a row each
believed themselves thorough and each missed instances, because the copy lives
in a dozen files and nothing compared them.

It has two tests, and the second one matters: "is actually able to fail" asserts
that the five rules still match the exact strings removed in US-111, US-156,
US-157 and US-159. A guard that silently stops matching is worse than none.
Demonstrated for real as well — injecting "Join 5,000+ agents - 4.9/5 rating"
into Pricing.tsx produced two findings and a failure, and removing it passed.

One bug in the guard, worth recording. The first version checked whether each
LINE looked like a comment, which flagged the middle lines of every multi-line
removal note — the notes quote the claim they deleted, which is the point of
them — and made the test unfixable without deleting the explanations. It now
tracks block state across lines.

Verification: build exits 0 (52 routes), verify:seo passes all 52, tsc --noEmit
clean. Checked the BUILT output too, not just source: a 248-file scan of dist/
for 24 banned strings returns only coincidental matches — "523" inside the award
icon's SVG path data and inside export-vendor's MD5 constants — plus the
legitimate feature description and the real computed ratings.

Full suite 624 passed / 23 failed at 127s, the heaviest-loaded run of the whole
session. Every suspect passes alone: marketing-claims 2/2, routes 3/3,
ContactForm 3/3, Register 3/3, Settings 6/6, SubmitReview 5/5, LeadDetailModal
7/7. The stable floor is unchanged — repo-hygiene x2, analytics, analyticsEvents.

## Platform Improvement Loop — 2026-09-09 (self-paced, 15 iterations)

### Iteration 1/15 — US-160: 17 MB of source maps were being published to the CDN

vite.config.ts carried `sourcemap: 'hidden'` with the comment "These are hidden
source maps that won't expose source code to users". That comment is wrong, and
it had been wrong long enough to survive US-125, which was explicitly about the
17 MB of maps in the build output and only reduced them.

`hidden` omits the `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment from the emitted bundle. That
stops a *browser* fetching the map on its own. It does not stop anyone else: the
map filename is the chunk filename plus `.map`, and the chunk filename is in the
network tab of every visit. `https://agentbio.net/assets/index-<hash>.js.map`
returned the whole TypeScript source — 193 files, 17 MB, 71% of a 24 MB deploy.
Every query shape, every RLS assumption, every route not yet announced.

The justification recorded in the comment was Sentry symbolication. Nothing
consumed them. There is no @sentry/vite-plugin, no `sentry-cli sourcemaps`
invocation, and no upload step anywhere in .github/workflows — `@sentry/react`
is the only Sentry dependency and it needs the maps on Sentry's side, not on
Cloudflare's. They were cost with no benefit attached.

WHAT CHANGED
  - vite.config.ts: `sourcemap: BUILD_SOURCEMAPS ? 'hidden' : false`, off by
    default. The comment now says what 'hidden' actually does.
  - The flag is a real escape hatch, not a formality: `BUILD_SOURCEMAPS=true`
    is what a local `npm run analyze` wants, and what a future CI job would set
    to upload to an error tracker and then delete dist/**/*.map before deploy.
  - scripts/check-bundle-size.mjs — already the CI `size-check` job — now fails
    if any .map reaches dist/assets without that flag. The check runs before the
    per-chunk budget loop so it reports even when a chunk is also over budget.

VERIFICATION, against real builds rather than reasoning about the flag:
  - default build: dist 24 MB -> 6.4 MB, `ls dist/assets/*.map` = 0.
  - `BUILD_SOURCEMAPS=true npx vite build`: 193 maps, as before.
  - the guard was demonstrated failing, not just written: dropping one .map into
    dist/assets produced the failure and its message, and removing it passed.
  - tsc --noEmit clean.

NOTED, NOT FIXED — `npm run size-check` is already red on main, and was before
this change: export-vendor is 605.0 KB against a 600 KB vendor budget (jspdf +
html2canvas). Same chunk hash before and after, so it is untouched by this work.
A CI gate that is red by default teaches everyone to ignore it, so this is the
candidate for the next iteration.

STORIES OPENED
  - US-161: `npx impeccable detect src` reports 65 AI-generated-design tells —
    49 ai-color-palette (purple/violet gradients), 10 gradient-text on headings,
    3 side-tab, 1 overused-font, 1 gray-on-color, 1 border-accent-on-rounded.
    CLAUDE.md names every one of these as a default to refuse. Not a lint fix:
    removing a purple gradient means deciding what replaces it, so it needs a
    palette and type decision taken first and then a page-by-page pass. Deferred
    to a later iteration deliberately, per the loop's own rule about work that
    does not fit in one.

### Iteration 2/15 — US-162: the Leads page loaded a PDF library to render a CSV button

Iteration 1 left `npm run size-check` red on main: export-vendor 605 KB against a
600 KB vendor budget. The obvious move is to raise the budget or add an
exception. Both would have been wrong, because the chunk was not lazy.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG. src/lib/exportUtils.ts opened with
`import { jsPDF } from 'jspdf'`. That module also exports exportToCSV, which is
a string builder and a Blob download and touches nothing from jspdf. But a
top-level import makes the jspdf chunk a static dependency of every consumer,
and Rollup cannot tree-shake it away because generatePDFReport in the same
module genuinely uses it.

src/pages/dashboard/Leads.tsx imports exportToCSV and nothing else from there.
Read out of the built output rather than reasoned about:
  Leads-CcCFikjE.js -> exportUtils-RdteEteH.js (3 KB) -> export-vendor (605 KB,
  184 KB gzip)
605 KB on the critical path of the most-visited page in a lead-generation CRM,
for a button that never calls it.

TWO MORE DEFECTS FELL OUT OF THE SAME manualChunks LINE:
  'export-vendor': ['jspdf', 'jspdf-autotable', 'html2canvas']
  - html2canvas is not a dependency of this project. It is not in package.json.
    jspdf references it optionally; the entry did nothing.
  - Naming jspdf there made Rollup place Vite's `__vitePreload` helper inside
    the resulting chunk, so consumers emitted `import{_}from"./export-vendor"` —
    a static import of 605 KB to obtain a 200-byte function.

THE FIX
  - exportUtils.ts loads jsPDF and jspdf-autotable with
    `await Promise.all([import('jspdf'), import('jspdf-autotable')])` inside
    generatePDFReport. exportToPDF and generatePDFReport are now async.
  - Both call sites await them. SearchAnalyticsDashboard's handler is async with
    a try/catch, so the toast follows the download instead of racing it and a
    failed chunk fetch is reported instead of becoming an unhandled rejection;
    ReportBuilder was already inside an async try/catch and just needed the
    await.
  - The manualChunks entry is deleted, not edited. A dynamically imported
    dependency does not need one — Rollup already splits it — and the entry was
    what dragged the preload helper in.

RESULT, from the build: export-vendor no longer exists. jspdf is a 386 KB async
chunk plus a 31 KB autotable chunk, fetched on click. The Leads chunk's static
imports contain no jspdf. exportUtils emits `import("./jspdf.es.min-*.js")`.
`npm run size-check` passes — 195 chunks, one documented exception.

THE TEST TOLD ME SOMETHING I WOULD HAVE MISSED. Making the functions async
without awaiting them at the call sites left `savedFilenames` empty and wrote
two real PDFs into the repository root — the exact US-121 defect the mock exists
to prevent, resurrected by an unawaited promise racing the test's teardown. The
suite caught it in the intermediate state. Both files were deleted; a clean run
now leaves the working tree clean.

The four PDF tests are awaited, and there is a new guard: two tests read
exportUtils.ts as text and assert no top-level import of jspdf or
jspdf-autotable, and that the dynamic form is present. One line restores this
regression, and nothing else in the suite would notice — the page still works,
it just costs half a megabyte to open. 10/10 pass. tsc --noEmit clean.

STORY OPENED — US-163, and it is worse than the one just fixed. The preload
helper has no home of its own, so with export-vendor gone Rollup moved it into
three-vendor (800 KB). FullProfilePage now emits
`import{_}from"./three-vendor-BHOYcAMp.js"` — a static import. That is
/:username, the page every agent puts in their Instagram bio, paying 800 KB /
220 KB gzip for Three.js before first paint whether or not the theme renders a
3D background. Before this iteration the helper was in the jspdf chunk and the
same page paid 605 KB for that, so it has been true continuously and only the
victim changed. It also makes check-bundle-size.mjs's exception text — "lazy-
loaded only on 3D hero sections, never on first paint" — false.

Attempted and reverted: adding 'vite/preload-helper' to the react-vendor array.
The object form of manualChunks resolves entries as package specifiers and the
build dies with `Missing "./preload-helper" specifier in "vite" package`. The
route is the function form of manualChunks, matching the virtual module id,
which means re-deriving every existing grouping by path and proving no chunk
reshuffles. Next iteration.

### Iteration 3/15 — US-163: Three.js was on the critical path of every page

Opened at the end of iteration 2 believing FullProfilePage was the victim.
Writing the guard showed it was worse than that.

THE MECHANISM. Vite's `__vitePreload` helper is a virtual module with no home of
its own, so Rollup files it into whichever manualChunks group it picks. It had
landed in three-vendor. Every chunk that lazy-loads anything then emitted
`import{_}from"./three-vendor-<hash>.js"` — a STATIC import of an 800 KB chunk to
obtain a 200-byte function.

THE ACTUAL BLAST RADIUS, from the guard run against the old config:
  FullProfilePage-B8_AhUTY.js  statically imports three-vendor (800 KB)
  exportUtils-D862ke8l.js      statically imports three-vendor (800 KB)
  index-PBqFv9Am.js            statically imports three-vendor (800 KB)
  jspdf.es.min-Ad-4HYgU.js     statically imports three-vendor (800 KB)
`index-*.js` is the ENTRY. It loads on every route. So every visitor to every
page on the platform — the marketing landing page, the blog, every agent's
public profile — downloaded 800 KB / 220 KB gzip of Three.js before first paint,
whether or not anything on the page rendered 3D. Before US-162 the helper lived
in the jspdf chunk and the same importers paid 605 KB for that instead. This has
been true continuously; only the victim changed.

THE FIX. manualChunks converted from the object form to a function. That is
forced, not stylistic: the object form resolves its entries as package
specifiers, so a virtual module cannot be named in it — putting
`'vite/preload-helper'` in the react-vendor array kills the build with
`Missing "./preload-helper" specifier in "vite" package` (tried in iteration 2,
reverted). A function can match the id directly, and does, first thing.

The groupings moved into a VENDOR_CHUNKS table matched on the package directory
a module resolves into. One deliberate difference from the object form: a
package's transitive dependencies are no longer welded into its group —
recharts' d3-* packages get their own chunks. That could have reshuffled
everything, so it was checked rather than assumed.

VERIFICATION, all against real builds:
  - helper now in react-vendor: `import{_}from"./react-vendor-DtYTAvso.js"`.
  - the only static importers of three-vendor are FloatingGeometry, GradientMesh
    and ThreeDBackground — the 3D components themselves.
  - FullProfilePage's static vendor deps: animation, form, react, state. No three.
  - the entry chunk's: charts, form, react, state, supabase, ui. No three.
  - chunk name set identical before and after — 195 both times, `diff` clean.
  - vendor sizes within 6 KB (react-vendor 155 -> 161.5 KB, the helper and
    react-router; three-vendor 818 -> 797 KB).
  - tsc --noEmit clean; vitest still resolves the config.

THE GUARD, and why the old one could not have caught this. The exception in
check-bundle-size.mjs said three-vendor was "lazy-loaded only on 3D hero
sections, never on first paint". That was false for months and nothing noticed,
because an exception made of prose asserts nothing. It now carries a
`staticImporters` list — the only chunks allowed to `import ... from` it — and
the check walks every built chunk and fails on any other static importer. A
static import renders as `from"./chunk.js"` and a dynamic one as
`import("./chunk.js")`, so matching on `from` picks up exactly the imports that
put a chunk on a critical path.

Demonstrated, not assumed: stashing the new vite.config, rebuilding with the old
one and running the check produced the four-importer failure quoted above.
Restored, it passes.

STORY OPENED — US-164. With three-vendor gone from the entry, what remains
static there is charts-vendor: 394 KB of recharts, in a chunk whose own comment
reads "Charts - dashboard only", loaded on every route including the marketing
landing page. Next iteration.

### Iteration 4/15 — US-164: the landing page shipped recharts to supply clsx

Left over from iteration 3: with three-vendor off the critical path, the entry
chunk still statically imported charts-vendor — 394 KB of recharts, in a chunk
whose own comment in vite.config.ts reads "Charts - dashboard only". The entry
loads on every route, so every visitor to the marketing landing page, every blog
reader and every public profile visitor paid for it.

It was not a stray chart component. All six recharts importers are admin or
dashboard files and all are correctly lazy. The entry pulled exactly ONE binding:

  import{e as Tr}from"./charts-vendor-DgQnpdXW.js"
  ...
  function X(...t){return el(Tr(t))}

`el(Tr(t))` is `twMerge(clsx(inputs))` — cn() from src/lib/utils.ts, which every
component in the app calls. clsx had no assigned home in VENDOR_CHUNKS, recharts
happens to depend on it, so Rollup filed it into charts-vendor and the entry
imported the whole 394 KB chunk to get a 500-byte function.

@babel/runtime's helpers had been adopted the same way. That is why three-vendor
statically imported charts-vendor: `import{_ as xa}` there is `_extends`, and
both recharts and @react-three/drei depend on @babel/runtime. Loading a 3D
profile theme pulled in a charting library to get Object.assign.

This is US-163's defect one layer down, and the generalisation is worth stating:
a tiny shared module with no assigned home gets adopted by whichever large chunk
happens to want it, and every consumer then pays for the whole thing. It is
invisible in a chunk listing — every size looks fine — and shows up only in who
imports what.

THE FIX. clsx, tailwind-merge, class-variance-authority and @babel/runtime named
in VENDOR_CHUNKS, landing in react-vendor, which every page loads anyway.

VERIFICATION:
  - entry static vendor imports: form, react, state, supabase, ui. No charts.
  - charts-vendor's static importers: Analytics, HealthDashboard, SEOManager,
    SearchAnalyticsDashboard. Dashboard and admin only.
  - three-vendor no longer imports charts-vendor.
  - react-vendor 161.5 -> 184.3 KB: four utility packages moving into a chunk
    that was already loaded, against 394 KB leaving the critical path.
  - chunk name set identical to iteration 3's; tsc clean; tests pass.

THE GUARD, generalised. US-163 added a staticImporters list to the over-budget
exception for three-vendor. charts-vendor is under budget, so it was not covered
— the enforcement was tied to the wrong thing. It is now a separate MUST_STAY_LAZY
map keyed by chunk, independent of size, covering three-vendor and charts-vendor.
Its failure message names the actual cause, because "X statically imports Y" does
not tell you what to do about it: look for a tiny shared module with no home and
name it in VENDOR_CHUNKS.

Demonstrated against the pre-fix config, not assumed:
  index-DyYjmFjj.js       statically imports charts-vendor (393.9 KB)
  three-vendor-9DsfYJow.js statically imports charts-vendor (393.9 KB)

Also removed a duplicated block in check-bundle-size.mjs — the budget loop and
its reporting appeared twice, the second copy dead. Introduced by an earlier
edit in this session, caught by node refusing to parse `const violations`
declared twice.

RUNNING TOTAL for a first-time visitor to any public page, across iterations
1-4: 17 MB of source maps off the deploy, 800 KB of Three.js and 394 KB of
recharts off the critical path.

## SEO loop — iteration 1/15 — US-165: four sitemap URLs the site did not link to

THE DEFECT. `npm run build` advertises 28 URLs in sitemap.xml. Four of them
were not part of the site's own link graph at all:

  /instagram-bio-for-realtors              24 inbound links, unreachable from /
  /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer            23 inbound links, unreachable from /
  /tools/listing-description-generator     23 inbound links, unreachable from /
  /tools/real-estate-agent-bio-generator    0 inbound links

Measured, not inferred: `vite build && npm run prerender` writes 57 real HTML
files, and the graph was read out of those files by parsing <a href> in the body
of each one and walking breadth-first from '/'.

The inbound counts are the trap. Three of the four looked well-linked — two
dozen inbound links each is more than /vs/beacons had. Every one of those links
was on a /for/{city} page. All 26 city pages carry noindex (US-153) and none of
them is linked from anywhere either: they link to each other and to the tools,
and nothing outside reaches them. An island linking to an island. Depth from the
homepage was the metric that showed it; inbound count said the opposite.

The bio generator is the one that stings. US-155 built it four stories ago
specifically to capture the ~180-impression "real estate agent bio" cluster that
US-152 took off the homepage. It shipped, it prerendered, it went into the
sitemap, it passed every SEO check in the repo — and no page on the site linked
to it. Submitting a URL is a request. Linking to it is what makes it part of a
site, and nothing anywhere was comparing the two lists.

THE FOOTER, which is where this was decided. It is the only surface that renders
on all 57 pages, so it is what decides whether a page is part of the site. It
was spending its links on:
  - three entries in "Resources" — "Real Estate Tips", "Market Insights",
    "Agent Guides" — all three pointing at /blog. Three anchors, three promises,
    one destination.
  - "Features" as `/#features`, an anchor on the homepage, while five real
    /features/* pages went unlinked.
  - /vs/linktree but not /vs/beacons or /vs/later, which ended up on 2 and 1
    inbound links respectively.
  - seven legal pages. /cookies had 56 inbound links — the most of any page on
    the site, more than /pricing.

Rebuilt as five columns: Product (the five feature pages plus Pricing), Compare
(all three), Free tools (all three), Resources (Blog, /for-real-estate-agents,
/instagram-bio-for-realtors, /press), Legal (unchanged).

DEAD ENDS. The three tool pages rendered neither PublicHeader nor PublicFooter,
so their entire outbound link set was 2-3 links. /vs/later had the same problem
where its two siblings did not. All four now render both.

THE GUARD — scripts/lib/link-graph.mjs, run by `npm run verify:seo`. It is a
whole-build property rather than a per-page one: no single page can be inspected
and found unreachable, which is why the existing per-page audit could not have
caught this and why every one of these four pages passed it. Only <a href> in
the BODY counts — a canonical, an og:url or a sitemap entry is not a link a
crawler follows for discovery, and counting them would let exactly this defect
pass.

Demonstrated failing before demonstrating passing, against the pre-fix build:

  4 of 28 sitemap URLs are not in the link graph
    /tools/real-estate-agent-bio-generator
        - no page on the site links to it — it exists only in the sitemap
    /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer
        - unreachable from / — its 23 inbound link(s) are all on pages that are
          themselves unreachable (e.g. /for/atlanta-real-estate-agents, ...)

One bug in the gate, caught by its own test rather than by the build: the first
version reported '/' as having no inbound links. It does not need any — it is
the entry point at depth 0. Reachability, not inbound count, is the question,
and the rule now checks depth first for every page including the homepage.

AFTER: 57 pages, every one with its own title, description and canonical; 28
sitemap URLs, all reachable from /, all at depth 1.

NOTE ON RUNNING THIS LOCALLY. The prerender cannot run in this sandbox without
two things that are not in the repo: a Playwright chromium build matching the
pinned version, and article rows. A throwaway two-article snapshot was written
to scripts/data/articles.snapshot.json to drive the render and deleted before
committing — it is placeholder text and must never ship (US-169 covers the real
fix). It did earn its keep: giving those two articles categories outside
BlogCategory's hardcoded map broke the entire build, which is US-166.

STORIES OPENED. US-166 (an unknown blog category takes the deploy down),
US-167 (no /tools hub, so the tool breadcrumbs claim a level that does not
exist), US-168 (InstagramBioAnalyzer's breadcrumb built from
window.location.origin, two items sharing a URL), US-169 (the article snapshot
the build documents as committed has never been committed).

PRE-EXISTING AND NOT MINE: `npm run test:run` is 2 failed / 656 passed on this
branch and on main. src/repo-hygiene.test.ts has been red since 908a2c1
(2026-09-04) put four markdown files and six shell/PowerShell scripts back in
the repository root, undoing part of US-121 and US-122. US-170 opened.

## SEO loop — iteration 2/15 — US-166: one CMS dropdown value took the whole deploy down

THE DEFECT, found by accident in iteration 1 and confirmed deliberately here.
There were three copies of the blog category list and they agreed by luck:

  src/pages/Blog.tsx        a hardcoded array of nine {name, slug, label}
  src/pages/BlogCategory    a hardcoded Record of eight slugs to editorial copy
  scripts/lib/articles.mts  categorySlugs(), which slugified whatever string
                            sat in articles.category and returned it

The third generated a /blog/category/{slug} route for ANY category on a
published article, including ones the second had never heard of. BlogCategory
renders those as a bare "Category Not Found" div with no SEOHead — no title, no
canonical — the prerender gate correctly refuses to write a page in that state,
and it writes all-or-nothing. So an article categorised "Agent Spotlight" did
not produce one bad page. It produced zero pages, `npm run build` exited 1, and
the message talked about missing titles:

  [prerender] 2 of 57 routes did not render:
    /blog/category/lead-generation
        - still carries index.html's default title (...)
        - no <link rel="canonical">
  [prerender] Nothing was written.

An editor changing one dropdown value takes the site down, and the error tells
whoever is on call to go looking at <title> tags.

THE FIX. src/config/blog-categories.ts is now the one list — plain data, no
React and no `@/` import, under the same constraint as prerender-routes.ts so
node can read it. Both directions of drift are now closed:

  - a category on an article with no page → not a route. Reported, not fatal.
  - a category in the registry with no editorial copy → `tsc` error, in
    BlogCategory.tsx, the file that has to supply it. categoryContent is typed
    Record<BlogCategorySlug, ...> rather than Record<string, ...>.

Reported rather than silent, because silence just trades a loud wrong failure
for a quiet one — an editor whose new category never gets a landing page should
hear it from the build, not from Search Console in six months:

  [prerender] 1 category value(s) have no landing page: Agent Spotlight (1 article).
              Those articles still ship; they just have no category page.
              Add the category to src/config/blog-categories.ts (and its copy to
              categoryContent in src/pages/BlogCategory.tsx), or recategorise them.

TWO MORE DEFECTS, found while fixing that one and fixed in the same pass.

1. The prerender's `**/rest/v1/articles*` intercept honoured `slug` and `order`
   and ignored `category`. Every prerendered category page therefore listed
   EVERY published article. Verified against a real dist rather than reasoned
   about — /blog/category/real-estate-tips contained an article whose category
   was "Agent Spotlight". The prerendered HTML is the only version a first crawl
   sees, so eight category pages were showing Google eight identical article
   lists. After: real-estate-tips contains "Tips One" and neither of the other
   two; market-insights contains "Insights Two" and neither of the other two.

2. An article's category was a bare <Badge>. Nothing led from a post to the
   other posts about the same thing — US-165's problem one level down. It is a
   link now, and only when the category actually has a page: the registry is
   what answers that, which is the whole reason it exists. An article in an
   unlisted category shows its category unlinked rather than pointing at a 404.

   Verified in dist: /blog/tips-one carries href="/blog/category/real-estate-tips";
   /blog/spotlight-three carries no category href at all, still ships, and is
   still linked from /blog.

Also replaced BlogCategory's article query: it derived the stored category name
by title-casing the URL slug, which round-trips only because all eight happen to
be plain words, and matched with ilike '%name%'. It reads the name from the
registry and matches with eq now.

VERIFICATION. tsc clean. 10 new tests in scripts/lib/articles-categories.test.ts,
including the old function verbatim as `preUS166Behaviour` so the test asserts
that the deploy-breaking route WAS generated and now is not. Three real builds:
one reproducing the break, one proving the warning path ships 56 pages, one with
three articles across two listed categories and one unlisted proving the
intercept and the badge link. verify:seo green on all of them.

## SEO loop — iteration 3/15 — US-167 + US-168: the hierarchy the site claimed it had

Both stories were about the same block of markup, so they went together. What
was actually shipping, read out of dist rather than out of the source:

  /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer
      BreadcrumbList: Home -> "Free Tools" -> "Instagram Bio Analyzer"
      rungs 2 and 3 both item="/tools/instagram-bio-analyzer"
      — relative, which Google rejects outright, and the same URL twice
  /tools/real-estate-agent-bio-generator
      "Free Tools" -> https://agentbio.net/tools/instagram-bio-analyzer
      — the tool NEXT to it, presented as its parent
  /features/lead-capture
      "Features" -> /features/property-listings, also relative, also a sibling

There was no /tools route in App.tsx at all. Three pages had been asserting a
level of the site that did not exist, in the one format Google reads literally.

53 breadcrumb problems across the build, on the first pass of the new rules.

THE HUB. /tools now exists, prerendered, in the sitemap, reading
src/config/tools.ts — which the footer's Free tools column also renders, so a
tool cannot be added to one and forgotten in the other. That is not a
hypothetical: it is exactly how /tools/real-estate-agent-bio-generator came to
be in the sitemap with no inbound link anywhere on the site (US-165).

/features did NOT get one. Building a hub whose content restates the homepage's
features section is the thin page US-153 noindexed 23 city pages over, so
/features/lead-capture's breadcrumb dropped the rung it could not honour and
goes Home -> Lead Capture. Two honest rungs beat three with one invented.
US-171 holds the open question.

THE COMPONENTS. Both breadcrumb components had the same three faults:
  - item URLs built from window.location.origin, which during the prerender is
    the preview server on 127.0.0.1. They survive only because prerender.mts
    rewrites that origin back out of every snapshot — a net documented as being
    for canonical tags and quietly loadbearing for structured data too.
    getCanonicalUrl() now, the same helper the canonicals use. US-172 covers the
    dozen other call sites that still do this.
  - seo/Breadcrumb.tsx generated its JSON-LD from `items` and rendered the trail
    from `breadcrumbItems`, the copy with Home prepended. On every page relying
    on showHome the structured data was missing the first rung a reader could
    see. Home is prepended before the schema is built now.
  - both emitted their own BreadcrumbList unconditionally, on pages whose own
    schema @graph already declared one. An `emitSchema` prop turns that off
    where the page owns the trail: 26 city pages, /pricing, /press, /blog and
    the two blog category pages were each shipping two.

THE ONE THAT WAS NOT A BREADCRUMB BUG. After the emitSchema fix, two pages
still had two BreadcrumbLists — Denver and Orlando, and only those two, which is
what a race looks like. The two JSON-LD blocks were identical except:

    dateModified: "2026-09-10T02:30:23.329Z"
    dateModified: "2026-09-10T02:30:23.352Z"

LocationTemplate set dateModified to `new Date().toISOString()`. React renders
twice, the timestamps differed by 23ms, react-helmet-async keys its dedupe on
the serialised content, and the page shipped two copies of the entire schema
graph. The duplicate BreadcrumbList was a symptom.

The disease is worse than the symptom: every city page was claiming it had been
modified at the moment of rendering, on every render, forever. That is the same
false-freshness signal US-149 refused to put in the sitemap — "a sitemap where
every lastmod is today is one Google learns to disregard". There is no truthful
dateModified for a static city page, so it says nothing now, which is what
sitemap.mts already does with lastmod. /features/lead-capture had the same thing
as citationDate; also removed.

THE GUARD, in scripts/lib/seo-audit.mjs, so it runs inside `npm run verify:seo`:
  - every item URL absolute
  - no two rungs sharing a URL
  - the trail ends where the canonical says the page is
  - every rung above the last is an ancestor of it
  - one BreadcrumbList per page

The ancestor rule needed an escape hatch, because Google allows a trail that
reflects how a reader arrived rather than how the URL is spelled — the 26 city
pages sit under /for/{city} with /for-real-estate-agents as their conceptual
parent. It is declared in DELIBERATE_NON_PATH_PARENTS, in code. An exception
made of prose asserts nothing; that is the lesson from the three-vendor bundle
exception in US-163.

The ancestor rule is the one that earns its place. The sibling-parent trail on
the bio generator has no relative URL, no duplicate URL, and ends at its own
canonical — every cheaper check passes it. There is a test that asserts exactly
that before asserting the ancestor rule catches it.

VERIFICATION: 53 breadcrumb problems before, 0 after, against real builds both
times. tsc clean. 8 new tests in seo-audit.test.ts. 58 pages, 29 sitemap URLs,
all reachable. STORIES OPENED: US-171, US-172.

## SEO loop — iteration 4/15 — US-172: every canonical was whatever host served the page

The story was opened in iteration 3 as tidiness — "a dozen call sites should use
the helper". That framing was wrong, and the measurement is what showed it.

getBaseUrl() in seo.config.ts was getSafeOrigin(), which in a browser is
window.location.origin. Around thirty call sites bypassed it and read
window.location.origin directly. So every canonical, every og:url and every
JSON-LD url/@id on every site-owned page was whatever host served the request.

On agentbio.net that is right by coincidence. The exposure:

  Cloudflare Pages gives every branch a *.pages.dev preview URL, serving the
  whole site. The prerendered HTML carries the correct canonical, because
  prerender.mts rewrites its own preview origin out of every snapshot. Then the
  bundle hydrates and react-helmet-async replaces it with the pages.dev host.
  Googlebot renders JavaScript. That is a preview deployment declaring itself
  the original of every page on the site.

A canonical is a claim about identity. It cannot be a reading of the current
environment.

THE SAFETY NET NOBODY KNEW WAS LOADBEARING. prerender.mts had one line:

    const html = result.html.split(PREVIEW_ORIGIN).join(SITE_ORIGIN);

documented as being for canonicals. It was silently holding up the entire
structured-data layer as well, and it only runs at build time, so it protected
the first crawl and nothing after it. It now counts what it moves and says so.
Measured across real builds:

    before:  moved 671 preview-server URL(s) on 58 page(s)   [every page]
    after:   0 preview-server URLs needed moving

671, not the dozen the story guessed. Worth stating plainly: the guess was off
by fifty times, and only building it twice showed that.

The counter earned its keep immediately. After the first sweep it still reported
7 on one page — the homepage, whose WebSite and Organization @ids and canonical
all came off `getSafeOrigin()` in a spot the grep for window.location.origin
never touched. A sweep finds what you search for; a measurement finds what is
there.

WHERE THE VISITOR'S HOST IS STILL RIGHT, and says so at each site:
  - /:username and /p/{slug} — a tenant may serve these from their own
    custom_domain, and there the visitor's host IS the canonical one.
  - Stripe successUrl/cancelUrl, OAuth redirectTo, the dashboard's
    copy-your-link UI. Those want the host the user is actually on.

THE GUARD, two tests:
  - src/config/seo-origin.test.ts puts the page on
    https://feature-branch.agentbio-net.pages.dev and asserts the canonical does
    not move.
  - src/config/seo-origin-sources.test.ts asserts no file in the SEO layer
    mentions window.location.origin or getSafeOrigin at all, with an exception
    list that carries a reason per entry and a test that each exception is still
    needed. Demonstrated failing by reintroducing the pattern in
    features/Testimonials.tsx, then restored.

    src/pages/Pricing.tsx is deliberately NOT in the covered list: it builds
    Stripe return URLs from the visitor's host, so covering it would mean a
    blanket exception, and a blanket exception on a page that has a canonical is
    worse than no coverage — it reads as checked.

VERIFICATION: tsc clean, 58 pages, 29 sitemap URLs all reachable, verify:seo
green, 671 -> 0 against real builds.

## SEO loop — iteration 5/15 — US-173: the claims US-159 could not see

This iteration started as a broad survey of the shipped HTML rather than a
story from the backlog: title and description lengths, h1 counts, heading
skips, og:image coverage, alt text. Most of it came back clean or trivial —
9 indexable pages with titles over 60 characters, one over 65. What the survey
actually turned up was a meta description on /vs/later reading "convert 3-5x
more leads than Later's generic link in bio tool".

US-159, eight stories ago, was the THIRD sweep for fabricated marketing copy
and shipped a guard to stop a fourth being needed. This is the fourth.

WHY THE GUARD DID NOT CATCH IT. Its rules encode the shapes the previous three
sweeps found: a named testimonial with an em-dash, a customer count, an x/5 star
rating, closings and sales figures, a competitor named as a customer. Nothing
about multipliers. So all of this was live:

  HeroSection.tsx, the default description of the component every marketing
  page renders:
      "ML-scored leads convert 2x better. Agents save 5+ hours per week.
       Close deals 30% faster."
  /vs/later, five times — body copy, a comparison card, the meta description,
  the on-page FAQ, and the FAQPage JSON-LD answer Google renders as a rich
  result:
      "3-5x higher conversion rates"
  The dashboard insights widget, telling paying agents:
      "Profiles with property listings get 3x more leads"
      "Agents with 5+ listings convert 40% better"
  /features/testimonials:
      "Video testimonials convert 2x better than text"
      "Video testimonials are 10x more powerful than text"
  The bio analyzer email drip, as a subject line:
      "The Instagram bio mistake 73% of agents make"

A number attached to an outcome is a measurement. If there is no query behind
it, it is not a measurement, whatever units it is in.

THE TESTIMONIALS US-159 HALF-FIXED. On the listing description generator it
deleted the names under three quotes and left the quotes:

      "My listings get 3x more engagement since using the family-friendly
       style. Game changer."
      {/* "— Jennifer L., Denver" removed (US-159). */}

Taking the name off an invented testimonial does not make it true. It makes it
anonymous, and an anonymous one reads as real feedback somebody chose not to
attribute. All three removed.

And because that rule wanted an em-dash, an entire section on
/features/calendar-booking — "What Agents Say About Automated Booking", two
testimonials attributed to "Jessica T., Luxury Agent, Scottsdale AZ" and
"Marcus L., Team Leader, Denver CO" — was never looked at. That markup puts the
name in its own <p> with no dash. Removed, and the rule now matches the shape.

WHAT THE NEW RULES FOUND BY THEMSELVES, on their first run, in a file no reading
had gone near — src/lib/instagram-bio-analyzer/scoring.ts, which produces the
personalised result the tool shows a user:

    "AgentBio captures 3X more leads than Linktree for agents"

  An unsubstantiated comparative claim about a named competitor, delivered as
  the tool's own advice. That is the most exposed form this defect takes.

    "Top performers in your area score 50+ points higher, which translates to
     3-5X more leads."

  Every branch of getCompetitiveComparison() compared the reader to a
  population the tool has never measured — "the top 5% of agents on Instagram",
  "top agents in your market", "in your area". There is no corpus of agent bios,
  no market segmentation and no lead data. It is a deterministic rubric of six
  checks, so it now says which of the six the bio is missing, which is the thing
  it actually knows.

OUT OF SCOPE, deliberately and in writing: BlogCategory's FAQ copy says school
districts "command premium prices (10-20% higher)". That is a claim about the
housing market, not about AgentBio. Editorial accuracy is a different job with a
different check, and conflating them would either exempt product claims or ban
the blog from citing a figure. It is in ALLOWED_FILES with that reason.

THE PATTERN WORTH NAMING. Four sweeps now, each thorough, each missing
instances. The first three looked; this one and US-159 wrote rules. The
difference showed up immediately — the rules found two claims in a file nobody
had thought to open. A reading finds what you look at. A rule finds what is
there.

## SEO loop — iteration 6/15 — US-174: a size no code had ever measured

Found in the iteration 5 survey, by reading the PNG header instead of trusting
the tag. Four SEO components each hardcoded, right next to the URL:

    <meta property="og:image" content=".../Cover.png" />
    <meta property="og:image:width"  content="1200" />
    <meta property="og:image:height" content="630" />

Cover.png is 1536x1024. A 1.5 aspect ratio, declared as 1.905. Facebook,
LinkedIn, Slack and X read those numbers to reserve layout before the bytes
arrive, so every unfurl of 52 of the 58 pages reserved a shape the image does
not have.

THE SHARPER HALF. ArticleSEO asserted the same 1200x630 for whatever
featured_image_url an article carries — an arbitrary upload — including inside
the BlogPosting JSON-LD:

    image: { '@type': 'ImageObject', url: socialImage, width: 1200, height: 630 }

Google reads ImageObject width and height to decide large-image rich-result
eligibility, which wants 1200px or more, and then fetches the image and measures
it. Claiming 1200 for an upload that might be 600 is not a rounding error; it is
a false eligibility claim about a file the crawler is about to check. Two more
places did the same thing: SchemaMarkup for any caller-supplied image, and
BlogArticle in microdata on the <img> element itself.

THE RULE. State a dimension only for an image whose dimensions are known here.
For anything a caller passes, emit the URL and no size — Open Graph makes them
optional, and an absent number costs a placeholder while a wrong one costs the
card.

src/config/og-image.ts is that one place. src/config/og-image.test.ts reads the
PNG's IHDR chunk — width and height sit at a fixed byte offset, so no image
library — and asserts the constants match the file. Editing the numbers without
changing the file fails; replacing the file without editing the numbers fails.

WHY COVER.PNG WAS NOT RECROPPED. The obvious move is to make the file 1200x630
and keep the tags. It was looked at rather than assumed: the composition fills
the frame — the phone mockup runs nearly edge to edge, the wordmark sits on the
bottom line — and cropping 1536x1024 to 1.91:1 removes about 110px from top and
bottom, taking the wordmark and the top of the phone with it. Declaring the true
size is correct and free. Recomposing the artwork is a design decision, and it
is US-175 along with the question of whether pages with their own subject should
stop unfurling as the generic product cover.

THE GUARD, in seo-audit.mjs so it runs inside verify:seo:
  - og:image:width/height must match the file, for the images whose size is
    known here
  - no dimensions at all for an image whose size is not
  - the same rule for ImageObject inside JSON-LD, at any depth
  - one dimension without the other is a mistake either way
  - a page with no og:image at all

Demonstrated against the pre-fix build:

    52  og:image is 1536x1024 but the tags declare 1200x630
    52 image problems across 58 pages

Adding the "no og:image" rule broke four existing tests, which was the rule
being right about the fixtures: they were minimal head blocks with no og:image,
while every real page has one. The fixtures now carry what the prerender
actually writes.

VERIFICATION: 52 image problems before, 0 after, against real builds. Checked
the two paths separately by giving one placeholder article a featured_image_url
and the other none:

  /blog/tips-one      og:image = cdn.example.com/hero.jpg, no width, no height
  /blog/insights-two  og:image = Cover.png, width 1536, height 1024

tsc clean, verify:seo green on 58 pages and 29 sitemap URLs. Opened US-175 for
the artwork and per-page image questions.

A note on og:image:alt, changed in passing: it was the page title, which is a
title and not a description of an image. It is now a sentence describing what
Cover.png actually shows, for the default; a page supplying its own image still
falls back to its title, because nothing here knows what that image is either.

## SEO loop — iteration 7/15 — US-176: every URL returned 200, and returned the homepage

The last line of public/_redirects was:

    /* /index.html 200

Before US-147 that was harmless-ish: index.html was an empty shell, so an
unknown URL returned a blank document under a 200. After US-147 it is the fully
prerendered homepage. So agentbio.net/anything-at-all answered:

    HTTP 200
    <title>Link in Bio for Real Estate Agents | AgentBio</title>
    <link rel="canonical" href="https://agentbio.net/">
    ...the entire homepage...

and only became the 404 page once the bundle executed and React Router matched
`*`. An infinite URL space, every member of it a duplicate of the homepage,
every one of them a 200.

A client-side router cannot set a status code. No amount of work in
NotFound.tsx could have fixed this; the fix had to be in _redirects and in the
Pages Function.

WHAT THE PREFIXES MADE POSSIBLE. The catch-all had to go, but the SPA still owns
routes that are not prerendered — /dashboard, /admin, /onboarding, the OAuth
callbacks, /p/{slug}, /:username. Those are now listed explicitly. What is NOT
listed is the interesting part: /blog/{slug}, /blog/category/{slug} and
/for/{city} are dynamic patterns whose every real URL is prerendered to a file,
so an invented one now falls through to dist/404.html and returns 404. Same for
/features/nope, /vs/nope and /tools/nope, whose children are a closed set.

THE ONE SHAPE STATIC RULES CANNOT RESOLVE is /:username. A single segment is
indistinguishable from a typo without a database lookup — and
functions/[username].ts was already doing that lookup, for crawlers, and then
calling next() whether or not it found anything. So a crawler asking for a
misspelled agent handle received the homepage. It returns dist/404.html with a
404 now.

With a deliberate asymmetry, which is the part worth reading twice:

    if (profiles === null) return next();   // the lookup errored or timed out
    return notFoundResponse(context);       // PostgREST said there is no such row

Answering 404 on a failed lookup would turn a database blip into a deindexing
event for every agent on the platform at once. Only PostgREST answering "no
rows" is a 404.

THE 404 DOCUMENT. NotFound.tsx had no <title>, so it inherited index.html's,
and no robots directive. It now carries its own title, a noindex, and links to
/pricing, /blog, /tools and /for-real-estate-agents — a dead end offering only
"go back" wastes the visit and gives a crawler nothing to follow. /404 is a real
route now, prerendered like any other and kept out of the sitemap, and the
prerender copies it to dist/404.html, which is the filename Pages looks for.
The prerender's own "rendered the 404 page — this route does not exist" check
needed an exemption for the one route whose job that is.

THE RISK, AND WHAT STANDS IN FOR A DEPLOY. Deleting the catch-all means a route
in App.tsx that is neither prerendered nor listed in _redirects is now a broken
page rather than a working one, and Cloudflare Pages routing cannot be exercised
in this sandbox. src/spa-routes.test.ts reads App.tsx and _redirects and asserts
they agree in both directions: no route without a way to serve it, and no 200
rewrite for a path that has no route behind it. Demonstrated failing by deleting
the /admin rules:

    these routes are in App.tsx, are not prerendered, and no _redirects rule
    serves them: ["/admin/seo", "/admin/audit-log", "/admin/health", ...]

WHAT IS STILL A SOFT 404, stated rather than glossed. RESERVED_SEGMENTS in
functions/_lib/social-meta.ts lists segments the profile lookup must not treat
as usernames. Most are real routes. A few — /legal, /about, /contact, /help,
/support, /api — are not routes at all, and being single segments they match the
/:username rule and still answer 200 with the homepage. None is linked from
anywhere and none has ever been a URL on this site. /for is the exception worth
a rule: it is a real prefix with 26 children and no index, so it gets the same
301 to the homepage that /features got in US-149.

VERIFICATION: 59 prerendered pages plus dist/404.html at the root, carrying
"Page not found | AgentBio" and a noindex. verify:seo needed the same /404
exemption the prerender did — its "renders the 404 page" rule fired on the one
route whose job that is, which is the rule working correctly on a route that
did not exist when it was written.

WHAT THE US-174 RULE FOUND HERE, on its first run against a full build in this
iteration: three pages ship with NO og:image at all.

  /vs/later
  /tools/instagram-bio-analyzer
  /tools/listing-description-generator

Each builds its own <Helmet> with a title, a description, a canonical and
ld+json, and no og:* tags. index.html ships static og:* tags, and on these three
pages they are absent from the output while the static twitter:* tags survive —
so their link previews had no image the platform was told about, and the
twitter:title and twitter:url that did survive still said "Link in Bio for Real
Estate Agents" and pointed at the homepage. Three pages, one of them the highest
commercial-intent comparison on the site, unfurling as the homepage or as
nothing.

Honest about the limit of the diagnosis: the mechanism by which the static og:*
tags disappear while the static twitter:* tags remain was not pinned down. The
prerender's dedupe only removes a static tag when a data-rh tag with the same
key exists, and there are none here. It was not chased further because the fix
does not depend on the answer — a page that cares about its own preview should
say so rather than inherit it — but that is an unexplained observation, not a
closed one.

[Followed up in iteration 8. Three things were established by measurement
rather than reasoning: index.html's og:* tags survive `vite build` intact, so
the homepage-seo plugin is not removing them; react-helmet-async does not
remove unmanaged tags, proven by /404, whose Helmet declares no og:* and whose
snapshot keeps all five static ones through hydration; and the prerender's
dedupe behaves as documented, removing a static tag only where a data-rh tag
shares its key. The original disappearance is therefore still unexplained. It
is no longer a live risk — verify:seo now fails any page that ships without an
og:image, which is the condition that mattered — but it is recorded as
unexplained rather than as solved.]

All three now emit the full og:* and twitter:* set from the shared constants.

The Pages Function reads dist/404.html through env.ASSETS rather than a plain
fetch, so an unknown username costs no extra subrequest — crawlers generate
those in bulk. Plain fetch remains the fallback for a runtime without the
binding, and if the document cannot be read at all the route falls through to
the SPA: a working page is worth more than a correct status code on a page
nobody asked for. All three branches have a test.

The existing test named "falls through for an unknown username instead of
inventing a card" asserted exactly the behaviour this story changes, so it was
rewritten rather than deleted, alongside two new ones covering the asymmetry
(lookup failed -> 200, no rows -> 404) and the missing-document fallback.

## SEO loop — iteration 8/15 — US-177: the file written to be quoted, quoting things that were not true

Started by closing the open question from iteration 7, then went looking. The
answer to the open question is in the note above: measured, not reasoned, and
still unexplained — but no longer a live risk, because verify:seo now fails any
page that ships without an og:image.

Then: public/llms.txt. It exists for one purpose, which is to be read and
quoted verbatim by AI systems, and nothing in the repository had ever checked
it. It is a text file in public/, so a sweep of src/ never reaches it, and no
component renders it, so no page audit sees it either. Three cleanups went past
it. Line 6 read:

    Used by 5,000+ real estate agents with a 4.8/5 star rating from 523+ reviews.

Those are the exact figures US-111 found, US-157 found again, and US-159 removed
from every component. Further down:

    Real estate agents using optimized link-in-bio tools report 8-12 qualified
    leads per month from social media (AgentBio data, 2025)
    Average AgentBio user captures 10+ qualified leads per month

The first one attributes an invented statistic to a named internal source,
which is the only thing worse than an unattributed one.

AND THE URLS. It linked to /features and to /compare/linktree, /compare/beacons
and /compare/later. None of those has ever been a route here; the comparison
pages are under /vs/. Since US-176 removed the catch-all, all four now return a
real 404 — so the file handed AI systems four dead links and, until last
iteration, four soft-200 copies of the homepage.

AND THE PRICES. Professional was quoted at $39/month with "unlimited listings".
src/config/pricing-plans.ts charges $49 and caps it at 25; unlimited listings
start at Team. The $29 Starter plan was missing altogether. So the number an AI
assistant would quote for the entry paid plan was wrong in both directions.

Also: the X and Instagram handles were twitter.com/agentbio and
instagram.com/agentbio, where the site links x.com/AgentBioApp and
instagram.com/agentbioapp. Two of the three free tools were listed, and neither
the /tools hub (US-167) nor the bio generator (US-155).

REWRITTEN, against the sources rather than from memory: prices and limits read
off the plan matrix, URLs taken from the routes the build publishes, tools from
src/config/tools.ts, handles from the footer. The claims sections are gone; what
replaces them is what the product does.

THE GUARD — src/llms-txt.test.ts, eight checks: every URL is a published page,
every price matches the matrix, no price appears that is not a plan, no user
count or rating or review total or lead-volume claim or multiplier, the handles
match, the comparison paths are /vs/ and not /compare/, every tool in TOOLS is
listed, and the file is long enough to be worth serving.

Seven of the eight fail on the file as it shipped:

    × points only at pages the build publishes   ['/compare/beacons', ...3 more]
    × quotes the prices the application charges
    × names no price that is not a plan          ['39','3000','15000','100','300']
    × claims no user count, rating or review total
    × gives the social handles the site links to
    × links the comparison pages at their real paths
    × lists every free tool

TWO BUGS IN THE TEST ITSELF, both caught by it failing on the honest rewrite it
was written to protect:

  - `[\d,]+` matches a bare comma, so "agents, realtors" registered as a user
    count. Every count pattern requires a digit now.
  - "100 leads a month" on the Starter pricing line is a limit the product
    enforces. "The average user captures 10+ qualified leads a month" is a claim
    about outcomes. The first version banned both. Only the second is a claim,
    and the rule now requires a claim frame — average, typical, report, capture,
    generate — before the number.

That second one is the more interesting: a rule that cannot tell a capacity from
a result would have forced the pricing section to stop stating what you get.

## SEO loop — iteration 9/15 — US-178: the company told Google it was somebody else

Followed from iteration 8. Fixing llms.txt meant checking its social handles
against the footer, and they were wrong. That raised the obvious next question:
where else does this repository state who the company is?

    sameAs, on every page, from two places:            the footer links:
      twitter.com/agentbio                               facebook.com/agentbioapp
      facebook.com/agentbio                              x.com/AgentBioApp
      linkedin.com/company/agentbio                      instagram.com/agentbioapp
      instagram.com/agentbio                             linkedin.com/company/agentbio
      youtube.com/@agentbio
      github.com/agentbio

Only LinkedIn is in both columns. The real accounts are @agentbioapp and
@AgentBioApp.

This is not a broken-link problem. schema.org `sameAs` on an Organization is a
claim of identity — "these accounts are this organisation" — and it is exactly
what Google reconciles an entity against when it decides what belongs in a
knowledge panel. Four of the six named an account under a handle this company
does not use, which either belongs to somebody else or does not exist. The other
two, a YouTube channel and a GitHub organisation, appear nowhere else in the
repository at all; there is nothing to check them against, so they are gone
rather than corrected.

A third copy of the same six sat in SEO_CONFIG.socialLinks, and
SEO_CONFIG.twitterHandle was '@agentbio', so twitter:site and twitter:creator
also named a different account on every page.

THE BAR, written into src/config/social-profiles.ts: an account goes in the list
only if the site links to it from the footer. That is the only evidence
available here that it exists and is ours. Claiming an account you do not own is
worse than omitting one you do — an omission costs a link, a wrong claim hands
the entity to a stranger.

THE LOGO, in the same node. SEO_CONFIG.organization declared logoWidth 512 and
logoHeight 512, and both Organization schemas shipped

    logo: { '@type': 'ImageObject', url: '.../logo.png', width: '512', height: '512' }

public/logo.png is 946x436. That is US-174 again, in the node that says who the
company is — and Google fetches the logo to build a knowledge panel, so it
measures it. ORGANIZATION_LOGO joins DEFAULT_SOCIAL_IMAGE in
src/config/og-image.ts, checked against the PNG header by the same test.

THE FOOTER now takes its four URLs from profileUrl(), which throws rather than
returning undefined — a footer link that quietly became href="undefined" is
worse than a build that stops. The markup and per-platform icons are unchanged;
only the literals are gone, which is what lets the two lists drift.

DEMONSTRATED against the code as it shipped, six checks failing:

    × lib/seo.ts names only accounts in SOCIAL_PROFILES
    × PageSEO.tsx names only accounts in SOCIAL_PROFILES
    × seo.config.ts names only accounts in SOCIAL_PROFILES
    × links every profile, so sameAs stays evidenced by something visible
    × is what SEO_CONFIG hands to twitter:site
    × takes its social links from the one list

ONE TEST BUG, and the same shape as iteration 8's. The first version banned any
sameAs URL ending in "agentbio" — which rejects linkedin.com/company/agentbio/,
the single entry in the old list that was actually right. A rule that cannot
tell the real account from the invented ones is not a rule about accounts. The
five wrong ones are named literally now, the way seo-audit names the 4.8/523
rating.

## SEO loop — iteration 10/15 — US-179: schema describing a site that does not exist

A URL inside JSON-LD is an assertion that the URL is a thing. Two were false,
and neither is detectable by looking at the URL — both are well-formed, on the
right origin, and named exactly what you would expect a real page to be called.
Only comparing them against the set of pages the build renders gives them away.

    7  structured data url points at /contact, which is not a page
    1  structured data urlTemplate points at /search, which is not a page

/contact came from ContactPoint in src/lib/seo.ts and PageSEO.tsx. The email
beside it is real; the page has never existed. A ContactPoint does not need a
URL to be valid, so it says the email and stops.

/search is the more interesting one. `SearchAction` inside `WebSite` is
specifically what Google reads to decide whether to render a sitelinks
searchbox, and three files declared one — Landing.tsx, PageSEO.tsx,
SchemaMarkup.tsx — against /search?q={search_term_string}. There has never been
a /search route in App.tsx. So the searchbox Google was being invited to render
would have sent people to a page that does not exist. Until US-176 that was a
soft 200 serving the homepage; now it is a real 404.

Deleted rather than repointed. There is no site-wide search here, and a blog
search is not one — inventing a target would have been the same defect at a
different path.

THE ONE THAT WAS WORTH FIXING PROPERLY. BlogListSEO declares its own
SearchAction, against /blog?search={search_term_string}. That claim was equally
untrue: Blog.tsx kept its search term in useState and never looked at the URL,
so following one of those links landed on an unfiltered blog. Rather than
delete the claim, Blog.tsx now reads ?search= — and ?category= with it — from
the query string. The schema becomes true, and a filtered view becomes a link
somebody can share. Typing replaces the history entry rather than adding one;
changing category pushes.

THE GUARD — auditStructuredDataUrls in seo-audit.mjs, run by verify:seo. It
walks every JSON-LD block at any depth, takes every same-origin string under
url, @id, item, urlTemplate, mainEntityOfPage or target, strips the fragment
and query — so #organization node ids and {search_term_string} placeholders
both resolve to the path that has to exist — and fails when that path is not a
page the build rendered. Off-site URLs are not ours to verify and assets are
files rather than pages; both are skipped.

Like the link-graph and og:image rules before it, this is a whole-build
property: whether a URL is a page is a fact about the build, not about the page
naming it. Seven of the eight occurrences were on pages that were otherwise
perfect.

Demonstrated against the build as it shipped: 8 occurrences across 59 pages.

VERIFIED, and the limits of it: driving the built site with Playwright,
/blog?search=Insights arrives with the search box already containing
"Insights", and /blog with it empty. That is the part that changed — where the
term comes from. The filtering itself is untouched code reading the same
`searchQuery`, and this sandbox cannot show it working end to end, because the
hydrated page re-fetches articles from a Supabase URL that does not resolve
here and ends up with an empty list either way.

  /blog                        input=""              
  /blog?search=Insights        input="Insights"      
  /blog?search=NoSuchArticle   input="NoSuchArticle" 

## SEO loop — iteration 11/15 — US-180: every article written by nobody

Started with a broad count of structured-data types across the 59 built pages,
looking for whatever was left. Three things came out of it, and only one
survived checking.

WHAT SURVIVED. Every article carried:

    author: { '@type': 'Person', name: 'Real Estate Expert', url: siteUrl }

"Real Estate Expert" is a job description. It was the default value of
ArticleSEO's `author` prop, so it was on every article the blog has ever
published, and it went out five more ways: meta author, article:author,
citation_author, twitter:creator, and a visible byline in BlogArticle.tsx
wrapped in itemProp="author" itemType="https://schema.org/Person".

Two things wrong with it beyond the name. The `url` pointed at the site root
rather than at any author page, so the Person is a human whose home page is a
marketing site. And twitter:creator takes an @handle, not a name, so that tag
was invalid as well as untrue.

Article.author is what Google reads to decide who stands behind a piece. A
Person who does not exist is the invented-testimonial defect of US-159 and
US-173, in the field where it counts most.

THE FIX IS NOT A WORKAROUND. An Organization author is a real thing: the
company published these, and schema.org has the type for exactly that. So an
article with no known author is attributed to AgentBio, in the schema, in the
meta tags and in the byline, with the microdata changed to Organization to
match. The `author` prop stays, so a real name can be passed the moment there
is one — articles.author_id exists, and resolving it is US-181.

THE GUARD, in seo-audit.mjs: a Person author whose name matches a short literal
list of roles — expert, team, staff, editor, admin, author, writer, anonymous,
guest — is a placeholder nobody replaced. An Organization named "Editorial
Team" is fine and the rule says so; the point is not to police names, it is to
catch a default that shipped.

    /blog/insights-two  BlogPosting names its author "Real Estate Expert",
                        which is a role rather than a person
    /blog/tips-one      same

Two here because this build has two placeholder articles; in production it is
every article on the blog.

WHAT DID NOT SURVIVE CHECKING, which is the part worth recording. The same
scan reported 26 pages with duplicate Organization nodes and 4 with duplicate
WebPage nodes. Both looked like the duplicate-BreadcrumbList defect from
iteration 3. Neither was: the Organization pairs are `publisher` and `provider`
references carrying the same @id, which is correct JSON-LD for referring to one
node twice, and most of the WebPage pairs are mainEntityOfPage references doing
the same. Counting @type occurrences is not counting entities.

One real residue: /features/lead-capture and /features/analytics each emit two
WebPage nodes with NO @id, so nothing can tell they describe the same page.
That is untidy rather than false, so it is US-182 rather than part of this.

Also added /logo.png to the audit's known-image sizes, so the Organization logo
US-178 corrected is now checked against the file by the build as well as by the
unit test.

## SEO loop — iteration 12/15 — US-183: the deploy contained things that are not the site

This iteration spent most of its time NOT finding defects, which is worth
recording as carefully as the ones it found.

CHECKED AND CLEAN:
  - Every page is either in sitemap.xml or carries noindex. 29 + 30 = 59, no
    page in neither and none in both. Sitemap exclusion and noindex are
    different mechanisms and it would be easy for them to disagree; they do not.
  - No indexable page is thin. The shortest is /blog at 408 words. Every one has
    exactly one h1, and no two share an h1.
  - Anchor text: 30 generic anchors across the indexable set, 29 of them "Get
    Started" pointing at /auth/register, which is noindex. One "Learn More".
  - The service worker is networkFirst for navigations, so it cannot serve a
    stale document. This was worth checking because APP_SHELL precaches '/' and
    '/index.html', and since US-147 those are the prerendered homepage rather
    than an empty shell — a cache-first navigation strategy would have served a
    frozen copy of the homepage to every returning visitor.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY WRONG, both in what gets deployed rather than in what the
pages say.

1. Two developer files in the deployed root. Vite copies public/ verbatim, so:

       https://agentbio.net/icons/generate-icons.sh
       https://agentbio.net/icons/README.md

   The script is a build tool. The README opens "This directory should contain
   the following PWA icon files" — a document published at the origin telling
   anyone who finds it that the site's icons might be missing. (They are not;
   all eight are there.) Neither is dangerous. Both are crawlable and neither is
   part of the site. Same shape as US-160's 17 MB of source maps.
