2. public/_headers still described the site as it was before US-147. Its only
   HTML rule was:

       /index.html
         Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
         Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, must-revalidate

   Every page is now served at an extensionless URL from its own directory, so
   no visitor requests /index.html and that rule applied to nothing while
   looking like a site-wide policy. There is a Cache-Control floor on /* now,
   which the hashed-asset rules deliberately override.

   Also in that file: /*.ts and /*.tsx, declaring TypeScript source to be
   application/javascript and cacheable for a year — wrong whether or not
   anything matches it, and US-160 removed the only mechanism by which source
   was reaching the deploy. /*.mjs, which nothing emits. No rule for /*.webp,
   which does ship. And /*.js matched /sw.js, telling caches never to
   revalidate the one script that controls whether a returning visitor ever
   gets an update. Browsers cap service-worker caching at 24 hours anyway, so
   that was bounded rather than fatal — but immutable is the opposite of what
   the file needs.

TWO JUDGEMENT CALLS.

The /sw.js rule goes AFTER /*.js, not before. Cloudflare applies every matching
rule and a later one wins for a header both set; a reading where the more
specific path wins gives the same answer from that position. Correct under
either interpretation, which is what you want from a rule you cannot test from
the repository.

The test does NOT ban rules that currently match nothing. A /*.jpg rule costs
nothing and is right the day an image lands. It bans rules that are wrong
regardless of what matches them, which is what /*.ts was. The first version
banned both and would have deleted forward-looking rules to satisfy itself.

Six of the seven checks fail on the state as it shipped.

## SEO loop — iteration 13/15 — US-184: the other half of the link-graph question

US-165 asked whether every page can be reached. It never asked the mirror
question — whether every link arrives — and the answer was no on the page whose
whole job is sending people into the blog.

Blog.tsx rendered a "Browse by Category" card for every entry in
BLOG_CATEGORIES, all eight. US-166 had already stopped generating a
/blog/category/{slug} route for a category with no published article. So /blog
was linking to six pages the build does not render:

    links to /blog/category/buying-guide, which is not a page
    links to /blog/category/selling-guide, which is not a page
    links to /blog/category/investment, which is not a page
    links to /blog/category/neighborhood-guides, which is not a page
    links to /blog/category/home-improvement, which is not a page
    links to /blog/category/general, which is not a page

Six of the twelve /blog links on that page. Each card even displayed its own
article count — "0 articles" — next to a link to nothing.

WHY NOTHING CAUGHT IT. /blog is reachable, in the sitemap, has a title, a
canonical, a description and no dangling structured-data URL. Every check built
in the last twelve iterations passes it. Reachability is a property of the
target; a broken link is a property of the source, and the two do not imply each
other in either direction.

AND WHY IT IS WORTH CHECKING NOW. Before US-176 a broken internal link was not
visibly broken: `/* /index.html 200` answered it with the homepage. A reader who
did not look at the address bar saw a working page, and a crawler saw a
duplicate of the homepage. Making 404s real is what turns this from invisible
into a build failure — the two stories only work together.

THE GUARD — auditInternalLinks in link-graph.mjs, run by verify:seo. Every
<a href> in the body of every built page must resolve to a rendered page, a file
the build wrote, or a path the SPA serves without prerendering. That last
category is not a guess: it reads the 200 rewrites out of public/_redirects, so
the link to /dashboard/settings from /privacy-choices is correctly not a defect,
and src/spa-routes.test.ts is what keeps that file honest about which paths
those are. Three guards now depend on each other rather than on prose.

TWO FALSE LEADS, checked and dismissed before getting here:
  - dist appeared to contain no CSS at all, which would have meant every
    prerendered page rendering unstyled until JavaScript ran. It was a `head
    -12` truncation in my own scan; the stylesheet is emitted and linked.
  - Article-to-article linking looked like a candidate. SimilarArticles works:
    /blog/tips-one links to /blog/insights-two.

## SEO loop — iteration 14/15 — US-185: answers asserted, answers absent

The FAQ visibility check has existed since US-157 and passes all 59 pages. It
checks that each question in FAQPage JSON-LD appears on the page. It has never
checked the answer, and the answer is the other half of the assertion.

    answers checked: 167   not on the page: 25

    5  /
    5  /pricing
    4  /blog/category/real-estate-tips
    4  /blog/category/market-insights
    4  /features/lead-capture
    3  /features/analytics

THE MECHANISM, identical in all five files:

    {isOpen && (
      <div className="px-6 pb-4">
        <p className="glass-body leading-relaxed">{answer}</p>
      </div>
    )}

Conditional mounting. A closed accordion does not have its answer hidden — it
does not have it at all. The prerender snapshots the closed state, so the
document served to a crawler contains the question, the chevron, and nothing
else, while the JSON-LD beside it asserts a full answer.

Google's FAQPage requirement is that the answer be present on the page. An
accordion is explicitly allowed; content that is not rendered is not the same
thing as content behind a disclosure. On /features/analytics and
/features/lead-capture the same block also carried itemProp="text" microdata,
describing an element that did not exist.

THE FIX: `hidden={!isOpen}` on the panel, which is present in the document and
not painted. Chosen over a CSS class deliberately — it is the platform
attribute for exactly this, it needs no stylesheet to be correct during a
prerender, and it is what assistive technology already understands alongside
the aria-expanded these buttons carry.

THE RULE now checks both halves. The test worth pointing at is not the one
showing it catches the broken page; it is the one asserting that the QUESTION
check still passes on that same fixture:

    expect(problems.some((p) => p.includes('question is not visible'))).toBe(false);

That is the whole explanation for how 25 answers survived six earlier audits of
this exact schema type. A check that covers half an assertion reports success
on a page that is half wrong, and there is no way to tell from its output which
half it looked at.

## SEO loop — iteration 15/15 — US-186: the guards could not see the pages the defects were on

The last iteration checked something it should have checked first: whether any
of this runs in CI.

It does. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `npm run verify:seo` on every push.
But the build step above it sets:

    PRERENDER_ALLOW_NO_ARTICLES: '1'

because CI has no database credentials, and that flag omitted the blog routes
entirely. So every check built in this loop — page identity, sitemap
reachability, structured-data URLs, internal links, FAQ question and answer
visibility — ran against the marketing pages and never once looked at /blog,
/blog/category/{slug} or /blog/{slug}.

That is where the defects were:

    US-184  six broken category links     on /blog
    US-180  a fabricated Person author    on every article
    US-185  8 of 25 missing FAQ answers   on the two category pages

None of those regressions could have been caught by CI, because CI did not
build the pages they were on. Three of the fifteen stories in this loop were
found in a part of the site the automation cannot see, and the automation
reported success the whole time.

THE FIX, without a new flag. PRERENDER_ALLOW_NO_ARTICLES already means "this
build will not ship", and a deploy is already forbidden from setting it. So
what it DOES changes, from "omit the blog" to "render three fixtures", and the
blast radius does not widen.

    [prerender] PRERENDER_ALLOW_NO_ARTICLES=1 — rendering the blog from 3
                FIXTURE articles, not real ones.
    [prerender] fixture exercises the unlisted-category path: Fixture Category
                That Is Not Registered
    [prerender] wrote 60 HTML files into dist/, plus 404.html

    [verify-seo] 60 pages, each with its own title, description and canonical
    [verify-seo] 30 sitemap URLs, every one of them reachable from /
    [verify-seo] every URL asserted in structured data resolves to a page
    [verify-seo] every internal link on 60 pages arrives at something

Run with no database and no snapshot, exactly as CI runs it.

THE FIXTURES ARE CHOSEN, NOT ARBITRARY. Each one exists to make a branch run
that only the blog has:

    fixture-choosing-a-listing-photo   a featured image on a host we do not
                                       control — og:image dimensions must NOT
                                       be asserted (US-174)
    fixture-what-a-market-report-...   no featured image, so the default social
                                       image IS dimensioned; second category
    fixture-an-unlisted-category       a category the registry does not have —
                                       the shape that failed the whole build
                                       before US-166

WHAT KEEPS THEM OUT OF PRODUCTION. loadFixtureArticles() is deliberately not
reachable from loadArticles(). A build that intends to deploy must never
silently fall back to invented content — that is the argument of US-169, and it
is why the real snapshot is still uncommitted. On top of that the loader
refuses any fixture whose title does not begin "Fixture:", every body opens by
saying the article does not exist, and the image host is under .invalid, a TLD
that can never resolve. If one of these ever escaped it should be obvious in
the first line rather than plausible.

DEMONSTRATED, and this is the point of the story rather than a formality.
US-184's defect was reintroduced into Blog.tsx and the CI path re-run with no
database:

    [verify-seo] 6 internal link target(s) have no page:
      links to /blog/category/investment, which is not a page
          from 1 page(s), e.g. /blog
      ...
    exit=1

Before this change that same build produced no /blog at all and exited 0. The
check was already written, already correct, and already running — and it could
not see the page. Then restored, and the CI path is green again.

---

## The loop, in one paragraph

Fifteen iterations. What changed is less interesting than what the changes have
in common: almost every defect was an assertion the site was making about
itself that was not true, and almost none of them were visible on the page that
made them. A canonical naming the host that served it. A breadcrumb claiming a
parent that was a sibling. An og:image declaring a shape its file did not have.
Six social accounts the company does not own. An author who is not a person.
Answers asserted for questions the page did not answer. Twenty-nine sitemap
URLs, four of which nothing linked to, and six links from the blog to pages
that do not exist.

The pattern in the fixes is the same each time: find the one place the truth
lives, make everything read from it, and add a check that fails when they
disagree — then run the check against the code as it shipped, because a guard
that has only ever passed has not been tested. Every story in this loop names
the number it found: 671 host-derived URLs, 52 wrong image dimensions, 53
breadcrumb problems, 25 missing answers, 8 dangling schema URLs, 6 broken
links, 4 unreachable pages.

The last iteration is the one that matters most for what comes next: those
checks were running against a build with no blog in it.

---

## Web platform loop — 2026-09-11 (self-paced, 15 iterations)

### Iteration 1/15 — US-197: every edge-function failure said "[object Object]"

supabase/functions/_shared/response.ts has answered every failure the same way
since it was written:

    { success: false, error: { code, message, details } }

`error` is an object. Twenty-three edge functions import those helpers. The
client that calls them, src/lib/edgeFunctions.ts, did this:

    errorMessage = errorJson.error || errorJson.message || errorMessage;
    throw new Error(errorMessage);

`errorJson.error` is truthy, so it won every time. `new Error(object)` coerces
its argument, and `.message` becomes the literal string "[object Object]".

That string is not an internal one. It is the `description` of the destructive
toast in BuyerInquiryForm, SellerInquiryForm, HomeValuationForm and
ContactForm — all four of the capture forms reachable from a public profile,
which is the platform's entire revenue path. A visitor who tripped the 5/min
rate limit was shown "[object Object]" where submit-lead had sent "Too many
requests. Please try again later." A visitor who mistyped an email was shown
"[object Object]" where validateLeadData had named the field. Settings'
username check, useArticles, useSocialMedia and the Stripe checkout helpers all
went the same way.

The code and the Retry-After were discarded along with the message, so no
caller could distinguish "slow down for 90 seconds" from "that email is not
valid" — the two failures a capture form most needs to tell apart.

WHAT CHANGED
  - toEdgeFunctionError() reads all three shapes actually on the wire: the
    standardized `{ error: { code, message, details } }`, the older
    `{ error: 'string' }` / `{ message: 'string' }`, and a non-JSON body.
  - A non-JSON body is shown only when it is short and contains no markup. The
    old code pasted `errorText` straight into the message, so a proxy's HTML
    502 page became a wall of markup in front of the visitor.
  - EdgeFunctionError carries `status`, `code`, `details`, `retryAfterSeconds`
    and `functionName`. It extends Error, so every existing
    `error instanceof Error ? error.message` caller keeps working and now gets
    a sentence instead of a coercion.
  - `retryAfterSeconds` is read from the Retry-After header OR from
    `error.details.retryAfter`, because rateLimitResponse sends both and a
    proxy may strip the header.
  - A REQUEST_VALIDATION_FAILED response names its fields. validationError()
    sends the message "Validation failed" and puts the useful part in
    `details`; "Validation failed" alone does not tell a visitor which of eight
    fields to correct. Bounded to five, because sanitizeFormData accepts forty.

VERIFICATION, against the shipped implementation rather than the new one:
  - Both fixtures in src/lib/edgeFunctions.test.ts are copied from
    rateLimitResponse() and validationError() verbatim. The bug was that nobody
    had ever run the client against what the server actually sends, so a test
    written from the client's assumptions would have reproduced it.
  - The tests were run against the code as it shipped: 7 of 11 fail there,
    five of them reporting the string "[object Object]". All 11 pass after.
  - tsc --noEmit clean. eslint clean on both files (the `any` warnings in
    edgeFunctions.ts are pre-existing, on the options interface and the
    EdgeFunctions helper signatures).
  - npm run test:run: 829 passed, 1 failed — see below.

NOTED, NOT FIXED — US-198. `src/repo-hygiene.test.ts > has no competing
edge-function build configurations` is red on main and was red before this
change: it bans `Dockerfile` and `edge-functions-server.ts` at the repo root,
and ce75af6 ("Restore the edge-functions build path deleted in US-122") put
both back deliberately. Either the restore was right and the test encodes a
decision that has since been reversed, or the restore reintroduced what US-122
removed. That is a question about how this platform deploys, not a failing
assertion to edit into agreement with the tree, so it is a story for the next
iteration rather than a line changed here.

### Iteration 2/15 — US-199 (and US-198): one POST to the lead form took the backend down

US-198 asked which deployment path is real. ce75af6 had already answered it by
measurement: functions.agentbio.net is Traefik-routed to Coolify application
isswgo8w4gs44ogk48wgsc88, which runs edge-functions-server.ts from the root
Dockerfile, and the Supabase edge runtime named as its replacement holds only
main/ and hello/. The router is production. So repo-hygiene was banning the
deploy path, and that is a two-line fix — ban the four genuinely redundant
configurations, and assert the two that ship are still there so the next
cleanup repeats the discovery rather than the outage.

Reading that file to answer the question is where the iteration actually went.

WHAT IT SERVES. The router carried a literal FUNCTIONS_MAP of 15 names. The app
calls 40. Twenty-nine answered 404 "Function not found":

    gdpr-export, gdpr-deletion          subject access and erasure — the
                                        compliance obligations
    create-portal-session               "Manage billing" went nowhere
    create-stripe-customer, report-stripe-usage
    verify-mfa, disable-mfa, get-sessions, revoke-session, login-security
                                        the entire account-security surface
    sso-initiate, sso-callback          SSO login
    submit-review                       the /:username/review page
    teams, api-keys, audit-log, send-welcome-email, optimize-image,
    health-check, pii-crypto, trigger-rebuild, and eight more

One mapped name, submit-contact, has no directory in the repo at all.

Until yesterday every one of those failures reached the user as the string
"[object Object]" — iteration 1's defect and this one compose, which is why the
404s could sit there. The router's 404 body is {"error": "Function not found"},
a string, so US-197 now surfaces it. Two independent bugs, and the second was
the reason nobody could see the first.

WHAT IS WORSE THAN A 404. The router invoked each module as module.default(req).
Five of the 84 functions export a default — check-username, generate-article,
oauth-proxy, publish-article-to-social, pii-crypto, and oauth-proxy even carries
the comment "Export handler for edge-functions-server (NOT Deno.serve)", so
someone adapted exactly five. The other 79 call serve() at module top level,
which is what Supabase's own runtime expects.

This was reproduced rather than reasoned about. Deno 1.42.0 — the version the
Dockerfile pins — was fetched, the image's layout recreated (COPY supabase/
functions ./functions, edge-functions-server.ts ./server.ts), and the server
started with the same CMD. POST /submit-lead:

    Error executing function submit-lead: TypeError: module.default is not a function
        at Server.handler (.../server.ts:87:42)
    error: Uncaught (in promise) AddrInUse: Address already in use (os error 98)
        at Server.listenAndServe (https://deno.land/std@0.168.0/http/server.ts:182:27)
        at serve (https://deno.land/std@0.168.0/http/server.ts:605:20)
        at .../functions/submit-lead/index.ts:59:1

    $ curl /health  ->  exit 7, connection refused

The 500 is returned, and then the process dies. The import ran the module's
top-level serve(), which tried to bind port 8000 — the port the router is
holding — and the unawaited promise rejected. Deno treats an unhandled rejection
as fatal.

So: an unauthenticated POST to the public lead-capture form takes down all 84
edge functions, and does it again to the restarted container on the next
submission. That is the platform's revenue path shooting the platform.

WHAT CHANGED
  - edge-functions-server.ts discovers functions from disk with Deno.readDir.
    A directory under supabase/functions/ with an index.ts is a function — the
    same rule the real runtime uses. 15 -> 84. The defect was never the fifteen
    names; it was that a person had to remember the sixteenth.
  - edge-functions-serve-shim.ts stands in for std@0.168.0/http/server.ts via
    edge-functions-import-map.json. Its serve() records the handler instead of
    listening, which is the same contract the runtime offers a function.
  - Deno.serve is intercepted for the duration of each import and restored in a
    finally, covering google-indexing and trigger-rebuild.
  - export default still wins if the other two produced nothing, so the five
    functions written against the old router keep working.
  - Imports are serialised: the shim's capture slot is process-wide, and two
    concurrent first-time requests could otherwise take each other's handler.
  - An unhandledrejection listener makes the class of crash survivable, not
    just the one cause of it.
  - The function's own CORS headers now win over the router's '*'. getCorsHeaders
    in _shared checks the origin against an allowlist; overwriting it with '*'
    silently widened every function that bothered.
  - /functions/v1/<name> is accepted alongside /functions/<name> and /<name>.

VERIFICATION, on Deno 1.42.0 against the image layout, not by reasoning:
  - /health: 84 functions discovered.
  - POST /submit-lead returns submit-lead's OWN response
    ({"success":false,"error":{"code":"INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR",...}} — there is
    no Supabase in the sandbox), and /health still answers 200 afterwards. That
    is the whole fix in one request.
  - Ten functions exercised across all three registration shapes, every response
    the function's own: trigger-rebuild 401 (Deno.serve), create-portal-session
    400, sso-initiate 400, report-stripe-usage 400 (top-level serve),
    check-username (export default), gdpr-export "supabaseUrl is required".
    Nine of the ten were unreachable before.
  - Zero "Error executing function" and zero unhandled rejections in the log.
  - src/edge-function-routing.test.ts run against the shipped router: 5 of its
    8 tests fail there. The reachability test parses FUNCTIONS_MAP out of the
    router when one is present rather than reading disk — reading disk would
    have made it pass against the very implementation it was written to catch.
  - tsc --noEmit clean, eslint clean, deno check clean on the new server.
  - npm run test:run: 92 files, 839 passed, 0 failed. The repo-hygiene failure
    noted in iteration 1 is gone, and it was fixed by deciding the question
    rather than by editing the assertion to match the tree.

NOT TOUCHED — CI type-checks functions against supabase/functions/deno.json,
which is a different import map. The shim must not apply there: a function
should type-check against the real module it will be given at runtime by
Supabase's runtime if this ever moves back to it.

### Iteration 3/15 — US-200: columns that do not exist, checked without a database

CLAUDE.md opens its schema section by saying not to guess a column name, and
gives the reason: gdpr-export queried a `blog_posts` table that has never
existed, coalesced the failure with `|| []`, and returned zero articles on every
subject access request without ever erroring.

That is the mechanism, and it generalises. PostgREST answers an unknown column
with 400. Almost every call site in this repo writes `const { data } = await ...`
and drops `error`. So the query does not throw — it returns undefined, and the
code carries on with an empty result as though the table were empty. A feature
built this way looks like a feature with no data in it.

`npm run verify:schema` catches this, but it needs a real Postgres and runs only
in CI. src/integrations/supabase/types.ts is generated from the applied schema
and is committed, so the same class can be caught in the unit suite in
milliseconds. That is what src/schema-references.test.ts now does: it parses the
Row shape of all 148 relations out of the generated types and checks every
`.from(...)` chain in src/ and supabase/functions/ — filters, write keys and
relation names.

FIVE LIVE FILTER DEFECTS, all in edge functions, all fixed:

  profiles.email            teams/index.ts
      The invite flow looked the invitee up by email to link an existing
      account. `profiles` has no email column — the account address is in
      auth.users, which is the entire reason _shared/agent-contact.ts exists
      (US-070). 400, error dropped, `existing` always undefined. Removed: the
      'accept' action already links the row by email, which is the only moment
      the invitee is present to be linked.

  articles.published        analyze-blog-posts-seo/index.ts
      The column is `status`. `data` was null, `posts` became [], and the
      function threw "No blog posts found to analyze" for every account that
      had articles. -> .eq('status', 'published')

  ai_models.model_type      optimize-page-content/index.ts
      No such column; the table has provider, model_id, model_name, is_active,
      supports_vision. aiConfig was always null, and the function's own error
      message is "No AI model configured. Please configure an AI model in the
      admin panel" — told to an admin who had configured one.

  seo_alert_rules.user_id   run-scheduled-audit/index.ts
      The table is global: conditions, rule_type, severity, is_active. No
      user_id. `rules` was undefined, so a scheduled audit never alerted on
      anything.

  seo_performance_budget.page_url   monitor-performance-budget/index.ts
      The column is `url_pattern`. No configured budget was ever found, so every
      check silently ran against the hardcoded defaults instead.

A DETAIL THAT MATTERS about writing this kind of checker: the first run reported
three of the five as still broken after they were fixed. Each fix leaves a
comment quoting the call it replaced — `.eq('published', true)` — and a scanner
that reads comments reports the explanation as the defect. It also invented a
sixth, profiles.user_id in pii-crypto, from a comment 45 lines below the query
that says why `.eq('user_id', user.id)` is needed. Comments are stripped first
now, replaced with spaces so line numbers survive. A checker that cannot tell
code from prose about code will be turned off within a week.

WHAT IT ALSO FOUND, AND WHAT IS DONE ABOUT IT — 59 write-key mismatches across
11 tables, every one in the SEO and Search Console subsystem:

    seo_core_web_vitals     12   stores lcp/lcp_pass; code writes lcp_value/lcp_passed
    seo_content_optimization 7
    seo_monitoring_log       6   has 7 columns; code writes 6 more
    seo_performance_budget   6
    seo_alerts               5
    seo_link_analysis        5
    gsc_keyword_performance  4   keys on property_id/query; code writes user_id/property_url/keyword
    gsc_page_performance     4
    articles                 4
    seo_semantic_analysis    4
    gsc_properties           2

Each is an insert or update PostgREST rejects, so these features compute their
results and throw them away. Telling a rename from a missing column needs the
table's intent, and some need a migration — that is US-201, not this iteration,
and it must not be guessed at.

So they are frozen in KNOWN_BROKEN_WRITES as a RATCHET, not an exemption: the
list may shrink and may never grow, and a fourth test fails on any entry that no
longer matches anything. Fixing one forces deleting it from the list. The debt is
enumerated in the suite rather than described in a document.

src/ has ZERO mismatches of either kind. The whole defect is on the edge-function
side — the side that never typechecked against the Database types.

VERIFICATION
  - The checker was run against the unfixed functions: all five filter defects
    reported, with file and line. Zero after.
  - Sanity assertions guard against the scanner silently matching nothing:
    148 relations parsed, leads has lead_type and not type, profiles has no
    email, 500+ sources scanned.
  - deno check --config supabase/functions/deno.json clean on all five modified
    functions.
  - npm run test:run: 93 files, 844 passed, 0 failed.

ALSO FIXED, incidental — tsc --noEmit was failing on src/config/og-image.test.ts
before this iteration's changes: newer @types/node types Buffer.equals's
parameter as Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>, which a Buffer no longer satisfies. The
PNG signature is compared as hex now. `npm run build:check` runs tsc, so this
was a broken build gate, not a cosmetic warning.

### Iteration 4/15 — US-201 (part 1): the Search Console integration was dead end to end

Iteration 3 froze 59 write-column mismatches in a ratchet and said each needed a
decision that must not be guessed at. This iteration took the Google Search
Console half of that list — four tables, 22 entries — and the decision turned
out to be easy, because the schema says plainly what each column is called and
one of the two Core Web Vitals writers already gets it right.

What was not easy to see is what the four defects add up to.

    gsc-fetch-properties    upsert sent site_url (a duplicate of property_url
                            under a name the table lacks) and last_sync_at (the
                            column is last_synced_at). PostgREST rejects the
                            STATEMENT, not the unknown keys — so no property was
                            ever saved.

    gsc-sync-data           therefore always answered "No verified GSC property
                            found" and returned 400. If it had got past that, its
                            own inserts named user_id, property_url, keyword,
                            page_url and platform on two tables that key on
                            property_id, query and url. Not one row would have
                            landed either.

So the integration has never worked, at any step, and every failure was logged
and swallowed: `if (!insertError) keywordsSaved++` counts to zero and reports
`keywordsSynced: 0`, which reads like an account with no search traffic rather
than like a broken write.

    gsc-fetch-core-web-vitals   twelve keys: lcp_value/lcp_passed for lcp and
                                lcp_pass, and so on. check-core-web-vitals writes
                                the same table correctly, so the right shape was
                                already in the repo, eight files away.

    analyze-internal-links      sent `url` for a page_url NOT NULL column. This
                                insert could not have succeeded even by accident.

WHAT CHANGED, beyond the renames — three things that would have been new defects
if only the column names had been corrected:

  - gsc-sync-data now resolves the property ROW and uses its id. It previously
    selected only property_url, because it was writing a URL where a uuid
    belongs. Passing propertyUrl explicitly is now checked against the account
    rather than trusted.
  - The day is deleted before it is inserted. The unique constraint is
    (property_id, query, url, date, device, country) and the request asks GSC for
    neither device nor country, so those arrive NULL — and NULLs do not conflict
    in Postgres, which means an upsert would have silently duplicated every row
    on a re-sync. Making a broken write work is where duplicate-on-retry
    defects are born.
  - One insert instead of one per row. That loop was up to 1000 sequential round
    trips per sync.
  - gsc-fetch-core-web-vitals writes data_source 'crux', not the column default
    'pagespeed'. This is field data from real visitors and the CHECK constraint
    has always allowed 'crux'.
  - analyze-internal-links now stores `issues` and `recommendations` themselves.
    seo_link_analysis has jsonb columns for both, and writing `issues.length`
    into a column called issues_count threw away the only part an operator can
    act on.

A GAP IN THE CHECKER, found by this work rather than by review. US-200's scanner
read `name: value` and missed shorthand: `{ url, device, lcp }` is three columns,
and `seo_link_analysis.url` — the NOT NULL violation above — was invisible to it.
Shorthand is matched now, and re-running the scanner found exactly that one new
reference and no others, so the gap was narrow but it was hiding the worst entry
on the list.

VERIFICATION
  - The checker was run against the four functions as they were at f014bc6:
    28 references reported. Zero after.
  - KNOWN_BROKEN_WRITES is down from 59 to 32, and the stale-entry test is what
    forced each removal — the list cannot describe work that is already done.
  - deno check --config supabase/functions/deno.json clean on all four.
  - tsc --noEmit clean; npm run test:run 93 files, 844 passed, 0 failed.

REMAINING, for the next iteration — 32 entries across six tables. Two of them
look like genuinely missing columns rather than renames: seo_monitoring_log has
7 columns and the code writes 6 more, and articles is written with seo_score,
seo_issues, seo_recommendations and last_seo_check. Those need a migration and a
types regeneration, which is a different kind of change from this one.

NOT DONE, and recorded — seo_core_web_vitals has no `inp` column. The table
predates INP replacing FID as a Core Web Vital. INP and the CrUX collection
period go into the field_data jsonb for now, which is the column that exists for
exactly that; promoting inp to a real column needs a migration.

### Iteration 5/15 — US-201 (part 2): a scheduled audit that died four different ways

The ratchet is down from 59 entries across 11 tables to 4 across one. What is
left is `articles`, which genuinely has no SEO-score columns — a migration, not
a rename, and that is US-202.

The interesting one was run-scheduled-audit, because it is broken at four
independent levels and any one of them alone would have been enough.

  1. The seo_monitoring_log insert sent user_id and check_type. Neither is a
     column — the table is a deliberately slim log (schedule_id, status,
     results_summary, started_at, completed_at) and both of those facts live on
     the schedule row it points at. PostgREST rejected it, `logEntry` came back
     undefined, and the very next statement reads `logEntry.id`. Every scheduled
     audit died with a TypeError seconds after starting.

  2. If it had got past that: all six audit helpers read
     `schedule.target_urls`. The schedule has `target_url` (NOT NULL, one) and
     `additional_urls` (text[]). `urls` was always [], so every loop body ran
     zero times and an audit that started would have produced no audits.

  3. If it had produced any: the alert insert used rule_id, related_url and
     metadata (none of them columns), status 'active' (the CHECK constraint
     allows open / acknowledged / resolved / ignored), and no value at all for
     `title`, which is NOT NULL. The rule's own fields were invented to match —
     seo_alert_rules has name, rule_type and conditions, not rule_name,
     alert_type and notification_enabled.

  4. And if an alert had been written: `if (rule.notification_enabled)` reads a
     field that does not exist, so it is undefined and no alert has ever
     notified anyone.

Four layers, and the outermost one made the other three unobservable. That is
what this whole line of stories keeps finding: the failure is never where the
symptom is, because there is no symptom.

THE REST, six more functions:

  send-seo-notification     wrote notified_at and notification_sent, which are
                            not columns, so an alert stayed 'open' however many
                            times it had been sent — and this function has no
                            idempotency of its own, so a retry re-notified every
                            channel. seo_alerts tracks this in `status`; a
                            notified alert is now 'acknowledged', and only
                            'open' ones are moved, so a human who already
                            resolved one does not have it reopened by a late
                            notification.

  check-keyword-positions   four reasons its alert insert could not land. A
                            keyword that dropped ten places raised nothing.

  monitor-performance-budget  six bad keys, plus `onConflict: 'page_url'` — not
                            a column, and url_pattern has no unique constraint
                            either, so there was no conflict target to upsert on
                            at all. Now an update by primary key or an insert.
                            Separately: FCP, TTFB and TTI were compared against
                            max_fcp_ms / max_ttfb_ms / max_tti_ms, which the
                            table does not have. `if (check.budget && ...)`
                            counts an undefined budget as a pass, so three of
                            eleven checks always passed and every compliance
                            score was inflated by up to 27 points.

  analyze-content           seven of thirteen keys wrong. It already computed
                            keyword_in_title and keyword_in_h1, which ARE
                            columns, and was not writing them; it does now.

  optimize-page-content     the AI response it pays a model to produce was
                            discarded on every run.

  analyze-semantic-keywords two independent reasons to fail: four wrong keys and
                            a missing NOT NULL primary_topic. Two values found
                            better homes than they had names for — the LSI
                            suggestions are literally co-occurrence data, so they
                            go in keyword_co_occurrence, and tf_idf_keywords was
                            computed and then never persisted at all.

A NOTE ON WHAT WAS NOT DONE. Several values have no column anywhere: the current
meta description, an analyzer's issues and recommendations, INP. The temptation
is to add columns and hand-edit src/integrations/supabase/types.ts to match.
types:generate reads a live database over psql and there is none here, so a
hand-edit would be a guess about generated output — which is the exact failure
mode this line of stories exists to stop. They are recorded in US-202 with the
decision each one needs, and the values stay in the response payload meanwhile.

VERIFICATION
  - The checker run against supabase/functions as of 7a09779: 35 references
    reported. Zero after.
  - KNOWN_BROKEN_WRITES: 32 -> 4, each removal forced by the stale-entry test.
  - deno check --config supabase/functions/deno.json clean on all seven
    modified functions.
  - tsc --noEmit clean; npm run test:run 93 files, 844 passed, 0 failed.

### Iteration 6/15 — US-203: the blocking type-check had never type-checked a function

A new axis. Five iterations have read this code; CI has type-checked it. Nobody
has RUN it. Deno 1.42.0 — the version the Dockerfile pins — plus the router from
US-199 makes that a twenty-line script: start the server, POST `{}` to all 84
functions, see what comes back and whether the process survives.

The first thing it found was not in a function.

    $ find supabase/functions -name '*.ts' | wc -l        # what CI checks
    110
    $ deno check --config supabase/functions/deno.json ...
    error: Relative import path "vitest" not prefixed with / or ./ or ../
        at supabase/functions/_shared/cors.test.ts:14:49
    exit=1

There are seven vitest specs under supabase/functions/_shared/. They
`import { describe } from 'vitest'`, a bare specifier Deno cannot resolve, and
`deno check` fails MODULE-GRAPH RESOLUTION before type-checking anything. One
error about an import path, exit 1, and not one function looked at.

The job's own comment reads: "Blocking: the deno-check baseline has been cleared
(114 -> 0). New genuine type errors in edge functions now fail CI."

Excluding the specs, on Deno 2.1.4 — the major version CI installs:

    Found 14 errors.
      7  backfill-lead-pii/index.ts
      6  stripe-webhook/index.ts
      1  trigger-rebuild/index.ts

WHAT WAS BEHIND THE GATE

  backfill-lead-pii — every response path. `getCorsHeaders(req)` takes an
  ORIGIN, not a Request, and the same confusion runs through the file: the
  _shared/response.ts helpers take the Request and derive CORS themselves, and
  every call here passed `corsHeaders` in that slot instead. Including
  `errorResponse('Admin role required', 403, corsHeaders)`, which puts a number
  where the error code goes.

  So the function could not return ANY response. Success, admin-denied, error —
  each helper calls req.headers.get('origin') on a headers bag, throws a
  TypeError, and the catch calls handleUnexpectedError, which throws the same
  TypeError again. Confirmed by running it: the caller got the router's own
  "Function execution failed", and the stack was inside errorResponse.

  This is the US-086 PII backfill: the one-off that encrypts the plaintext email
  and phone on `leads`, which 20260901000001_leads_drop_plaintext_pii.sql refuses
  to run until it has completed. It has never been able to complete.

  trigger-rebuild — `errorResponse('Deploy hook rejected the request', req, 502)`.
  req in the code slot, 502 in the req slot. The failure path threw instead of
  reporting the failure.

  stripe-webhook — three helpers typed their client `ReturnType<typeof
  createClient>`, which is createClient's DEFAULT generic instantiation,
  SupabaseClient<unknown, never, GenericSchema>. What they are handed is what
  `createClient(url, key)` infers: SupabaseClient<any, "public", any>. Six call
  sites, all in the paths that resolve a plan from a Stripe price and load its
  limits.

WHAT CHANGED
  - The glob excludes *.test.ts, and node_modules, which --node-modules-dir=auto
    creates under supabase/functions and which would otherwise make a re-run
    check 198 files instead of 103.
  - The job fails loudly if the exclusion ever matches nearly everything, so
    "checked 0 files, exit 0" cannot become the new way to be green.
  - All 14 errors fixed.

VERIFICATION
  - deno check over all 103 files on Deno 2.1.4: exit 0. First time.
  - Runtime, not just types: POST /backfill-lead-pii now answers
    {"code":"AUTH_TOKEN_MISSING"} with 401, where before it produced a
    router-level 500 with a TypeError inside errorResponse.
  - The guard was run against the workflow as it was at 356b7da and fails there.
  - tsc --noEmit clean; npm run test:run 93 files, 845 passed, 0 failed.

NOTED, NOT FIXED — US-204, and it is the larger half of what the sweep found.
Of 84 functions given an unauthenticated POST, 24 answered 401 correctly and 20
answered 5xx — and for at least 14 of those the cause is the CALLER's missing
credentials. requireAuth throws a plain Error before it ever touches Supabase;
the catch hands it to handleUnexpectedError, which logs "[UnexpectedError]" and
returns 500. Six functions print "Unauthorized: No authorization header" with a
500 status; the rest return "An unexpected error occurred", which does not tell
the client it was an auth problem at all. 5xx is retried by clients, CDNs and
cron where 401 is not, so an unauthenticated caller becomes a retry storm — and
every auth failure looks like a crash, so a real outage cannot be seen against
the noise. The sweep itself should become a CI job: US-199's AddrInUse crash is
the proof that running a function finds what deno check cannot.

### Iteration 7/15 — US-204: telling a caller "you are not logged in" with a 500

requireAuth throws before it ever touches Supabase:

    const authHeader = req.headers.get('Authorization');
    if (!authHeader) throw new Error('Unauthorized: No authorization header');

A bare Error. Every function catches it in the same `catch` that guards against
genuine faults, and answers 500. The unauthenticated sweep from iteration 6
measured the result: of 84 functions, 24 answered 401 and 20 answered 5xx, at
least 14 of them for this reason.

Two things that costs, and neither is cosmetic:

  - 5xx is retried. Browsers, CDNs, cron runners and webhook senders all treat
    it as "the server is having a moment" and come back. 401 they do not. An
    expired session became a retry loop against a function that was working
    perfectly.
  - Every auth failure looks like a crash. The logs fill with [UnexpectedError]
    for requests that were simply unauthenticated, and a platform that cannot
    see a real outage against that noise has wired up health-check and Sentry
    for nothing.

WHAT CHANGED
  - _shared/http-error.ts: an HttpError carrying its own status and code, with
    unauthorized() and forbidden() constructors. The decision stays where the
    knowledge is — requireAuth knows it is a 401, and the error handler should
    not have to infer that from a message string.
  - requireAuth, requireAdmin, requireOwnership and the two webhook-auth throw
    sites raise it.
  - BOTH error frameworks learned to recognise it. handleUnexpectedError in
    _shared/response.ts was the obvious one; _shared/errors.ts has a second,
    older handleError with its own AppError hierarchy, which google-indexing
    uses and which had the identical hole. Fixing one would have left the other.
  - 25 functions hand-roll their catch rather than calling either, so
    `status: 500` became `status: errorStatus(error)`. Rewriting them to the
    standard envelope would change what their callers parse; changing the status
    alone fixes the defect without touching the contract.
  - send-listing-generator-email threw a bare Error for a missing email address,
    which the same catch turned into a 500. A form submitted without an email
    was reported as a server fault and retried. Now 400.

MEASURED, not argued — the same sweep, before and after:

                       before      after
      401                 24         39
      400                 29         29
      429                  9          9
      5xx                 20          5

The five remaining are honest: three want a server-side API key that is genuinely
absent, health-check correctly answers 503 with no database behind it, and
google-indexing now answers 401.

THE DURABLE PART. scripts/smoke-edge-functions.mjs makes the sweep repeatable —
`npm run smoke:functions` — and it is a CI job now. Its three assertions are the
three findings of this loop, in order:

    the router must discover the full set        US-199, the 15-of-84 map
    no function may answer 5xx unauthenticated   US-204, this story
    the router must survive the sweep            US-199, the AddrInUse crash

The third matters more than it looks. US-199's crash returned a 500 for the
request that caused it and THEN killed the process, so a check that only looked
at each response would have passed it.

No database is needed for any of this: a function that reaches its own auth or
validation check has already proved it imports, registers a handler and returns
a Response — which is exactly what deno check cannot tell you.

VERIFICATION
  - Against supabase/functions as of bef2983 the script names 16 functions and
    exits 1. Against this tree it exits 0.
  - A first draft used process.exit(1) on the failure path, which races the
    cleanup and leaves a router holding the port — so the NEXT run failed with
    "the router did not survive the sweep" on a tree that was fine. It sets
    exitCode and lets the finally reap the child instead. A flaky guard is worse
    than none; this one was flaky for about four minutes.
  - deno check over all 104 files on Deno 2.1.4: exit 0.
  - tsc --noEmit clean; npm run test:run 93 files, 845 passed, 0 failed.
